I am sorry to delay ithe proceedings, but it seems to me that before we prorogue we should have a statement from the government with regard to our foreign relations, and also an explanation of what has been done since the last Imperial conference to implement its decisions. I am still more sorry to have to bring this matter up in the form of a motion of want of confidence. There is just a sufficient degree of diffidence or disquietude regarding the course of the government to make it sincere on my part; but if I resort to this procedure, iit is rather because the regulations of the house prevent any individual member bringing an important subject before the 'house unless it is in this form. Thus I will have to conclude these remarks with a motion of regret at the course followed, or rather the lack of action on the part of this government and other governments represented at the Imperial conference, in not giving full sanction to the decisions arrived at in London.
In the report of the conference, the following statement appears:
Every self-governing dominion of the empire is now' the master of its destiny. In fact, if not always in form, it is subject to no compulsion whatever.
Further on:
Equality of status, so far as Great Britain and the dominions are concerned, is thus the root principle governing our inter-imperial relations.
Is it not important for all concerned that " forms " should be made to coincide as exactly as possible with " facts," but still more so with the " root principle " thus stated emphatically by the conference to be now the basis of inter-imperial relations, and therefore the basis of external relations of each individual member of the so-called British commonwealth of nations with foreign countries? Of " compulsion " it was rather useless to speak. For many years past, the British government can be absolved from any attempt at exercising compulsion on any of the dominion governments in any matter political, whether in internal or in external affairs. But there are oertainly still in existence limitations over the exercise of our full sovereign powers, either in internal or external matters;
3446	COMMONS
Foreign Relations-Mr. Bourassa
and, what is perhaps worse still, there are loopholes and equivocations that were not dispelled at the last Imperial conference, and which, I think, should be clarified as soon as possible. If full and individual freedom of action is now the constitutional basis of government in each of the self governing nations acknowledging King George as their sovereign, then all obstacles preventing the full and unhampered exercise of that freedom should be removed, and points which are still obscure should be clarified in order to dispel in the present and to avoid in the future all possible misunderstanding between Great Britain, Canada and the other self-governing dominions or sister nations, call them by whatever name you like, or between each of those countries and any foreign country with which it may have to deal.
As regards the head of our government it was stipulated at the last Imperial conference :
It is an essential consequence of the equality of status existing among the members of the British commonwealth of nations that the governor general of a dominion is the representative of the crown holding in all essential respects the same position in relation to the administration of public affairs in the dominion as is held by His Majesty the King in Great Britain, and that he is not the representative or agent of His Majesty's government in Great Britain or of any department of that government.
Further:
It seemed to us to follow that the practice whereby the governor general of a dominion is the formal official channel of communication between His Majesty's government in Great Britain and his governments in the dominions might be regarded as no longer wholly in accordance with the constitutional position of the governor general. It was thought that the recognized official channel of communication should be, in future, between government and government direct.
This was adopted in the month of October, 1926, and to my great surprise, in taking cognizance of the papers deposited on the table during this session, relating to the rupture between Canada and Russia which took place in May, 1927, seven months afterwards, I noticed that all the correspondence exchanged between the Canadian government and the British government was exchanged through His Excellency the Governor General. Therefore, I hope the Prime Minister will explain to the house why, seven months after the adoption of this resolution, it was not put into effect in a matter of this importance. May I suggest, just in passing, in order to make the position clear both to the people of Canada and to the people in the other British communities as well as to the foreign world, that the Governor General being no more a governor should
Mr. Bourassa.]
receive the title and dignity of Viceroy, bo that it would be made quite clear that the Governor General occupies, as was stated in London a year ago last fall, the same position, enjoys the same privileges, and is limited to the same extent in the exercise of his functions, as His Majesty the King is in Great Britain.
A matter that was considered at the conference was the reservation of dominion legislation for the assent of His Majesty, or for the disallowance of such legislation. This is now a pure matter of form. Another question was the jurisdiction of the dominions outside of their own territory, what is known generally as extra-Territorial jurisdiction. This is an important matter. Another was the revision of the Colonial Laws Validity Act This act was invoked not long ago by the Privy Council in London to annul a statute of Canada which had been in force for years and years and respected by all Canadian tribunals. It was wiped off by a stroke of the pen, not because of the situation of Canada, but because of the possible application of the precedent to Ireland. This is, I think, a very important matter. These three subjects were to be submitted to the study of a committee. I should like to know, and I think the house will be interested in learning from the Prime Minister, who is at the same time Minister of External Affairs, whethei that committee has been appointed, of whom it will be composed, what questions will be referred to it, what directions will be given to the representatives of Canada upon it and when we may expect to have a report therefrom. That committee was supposed to enlighten itself, with the help of experts on various matters of legislation, and therefore to be in a position to report to the various governments in a very informed way.
Then the important matter of merchant shipping laws was to be submitted to a subconference which was to sit at the same time as this committee, with its array of experts, so, I suppose, that both bodies could help each other. I would respectfully ask the Prime Minister to tell us when the sub-conference is going to convene, how it will be composed, what will be the various matters submitted to it and when we may expect or hope for a report.
The matter of appeals to the Privy Council has been practically left in the hands of each parliament of the various dominions. It is not so stated in so many words, but it is easy to read between the lines of the paragraph of the report relating thereto, that all the members of that conference acknowledged or asserted the right of each so-called sister nation

Foreign Relations-Mr. Bourassa
composing the British commonwealth to deal with this matter as it thought fit. I aim not going to touch upon this point at all, because in itself it would require very wide consideration. I simply beg the government, when they take it up, to read carefully the debate which took place not very long ago in the House of Lords relating to the decision of that semi-judicial, semi-political body with regard to the payment of pensions to civil servants in Ireland. This may dispel the delusion that the Privy Council is altogether infallible either in judicial or political matters. I refer to the case of Wigg and Cochrane versus the Irish Free State.
But what I desire to bring more especially to the attention of the government- and the house is all that concerns our foreign relations. The conference has acknowledged broadly, in a spirit of true British statesmanship, the right of Canada, as well as of any other British dominion, to open and maintain direct relations with any foreign country, and to place itself in its relations with those foreign countries on the footing of a free nation. The government, quite properly, I think, has given effect to that decision, first by the appointment of a representative of Canada in Washington, an act now reciprocated by the appointment of an American minister in Ottawa; and very soon the house will be called upon to approve of similar action being taken with regard to France and Japan. I may say that the policy of the government in this connection has, though it does not amount to very much, my full approval, but it has also the full approval of all itrue-thinking Canadians. I simply give the friendly advice that in everything which relates to the material organization of the various legations, the government should not lose sight of the fact that Canada is still a small country, in importance and in population. The government should not undertake to put these foreign legations on the material footing of embassies from large countries. If we want to multiply those relations for the good of Canada, for the extension of our foreign relations, we must be in a position to establish such agencies or legations in every country with which we may have relations, and therefore I think it would be at once wise, prudent, modest and proper to be a little more economical in the display of material installation, and look for the multiplication of those agencies rather than make a few of them very costly and, may I say, parvenu-like.
What is extremely important is that before we go on multiplying our relations with foreign countries by establishing legations, we should have a clear and above-board understanding
with Great Britain on the one hand, and with foreign countries on the other, as to what will be the exact situation of those representatives of Canada in foreign capitals where the British government is equally represented by an ambassador or a minister plenipotentiary; and likewise, .as to what will be the situation of the representatives of .those foreign countries with us in regard, on the one hand, to our relations with Great Britain as a member of the so-called British commonwealth of nations, and on the other, in regard to the relation of those countries with the government of Great Britain. In order to make my point clear, I wish to bring before the house a sketch or short history of the establishment and rupture of our relations with Russia; and second, to take up the standing of foreign consuls representing in Canada countries which have not yet established direct relations with us.
The history of our relations with Russia makes very interesting reading indeed. It took birth first in the form of a trade agreement concluded on the 16th of March, 1921, between His Britannic Majesty's government and the government of the Russian Socialist Federal Soviet republic. That trade agreement, it is easy to see by reading it, was preliminary to the conclusion of a complete international treaty. In fact, in the very preamble it is said:
Whereas it is desirable in the interest both of Russia and the United Kingdom that peaceful trade and commerce should be resumed forthwith between those countries, and whereas it is necessary, pending the conclusion of a formal general peace treaty between the governments of these countries, etc.,
May I say, to soothe some disquieted consciences, that this trade agreement was not concluded between the Soviet republic and a Radical government in England, but by the coalition government of which Mr. Lloyd George was then prime minister, and signed by Sir Robert Home, a good, thorough, proven Tory of England. Canada, under an equally good Tory government, headed by Mr. Arthur Meighen. decided to adhere to that arrangement. Their first order in council was passed on August 22, 1921, upon the recommendation of no less a statesman than Sir George Foster, then Minister of Trade and Commence, and with the full approval of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. Arthur Meighen. lit did not materialize at once. A general election came on in the fall of that year; but the then Conservative government attached such importance to the establishment of those trade relations that before quitting office, they passed a second order in council, dated December 26, 1921, ; incorporating a formula prepared for them in London by the
3448	COMMONS
Foreign Relations-Mr. Bourassa
Department of Foreign Affairs, under which Canada declared that it adhered .to the arrangement concluded between the British and the Russian governments on March 16, 1921.
Now that created quite a queer situation. There was no reservation whatever on the part of Canada. It was not an adhesion to one section or the other of the treaty; it was not a mere acceptance of those clauses of the treaty which established trade relations alone. No, it was an adhesion to the whole treaty. It is, of course, too long to read, but I would advise every member of parliament who thinks of the general interests of the country once in a while, to read it through. They will find out that there were mutual undertakings on the part of Russia and England to clear the seas surrounding Europe of what mines would still be floating around after the war; it made very long and precise stipulations for the sojourning of their respective nationals in each country; it stipulated in what manner the official agents of each country should reside-the. Russians in England and the English in Russia; it stipulated also in what manner the property as well as the persons of the nationals of each country would be protected by their respective governments, and so forth. So that by accepting the formula written in London and sent to Ottawa, and accepted here, with eyes closed or opened-I am not quite sure which -by the Canadian ministers, we adhered to all those stipulations. I mention this merely en passant, to show how wise the Imperial conference of 1923 was when it stipulated that each government thereafter should negotiate for itself and according to its own needs the nature and extent of its relations with other countries.
The adhesion of Canada was communicated internationally by the exchange of those notes, which have been produced to-day by the Prime Minister after permission received from London. May I say in passing that there is something ludicrous in the idea that it should take fifteen days to get permission from either the Dominion Secretary or the Foreign Secretary in London to enable Canadians to take cognizance of a paper which concerns them alone. I quite realize, as the Prime Minister said the other day, that if we entertain relations with various governments, then when there is in the correspondence or the records matters of concern to those governments, it is an elementary rule of diplomacy and international etiquette than none of the governments concerned should make the documents

public without the consent of the other governments. But in this instance the British government acted, as Lord Haldane defined it many years ago, merely as a trustee, so to speak, for the Dominion of Canada; and therefore this document should have been a Canadian document, not to be made public without the consent of the Russian government so long as our friendly relations continued; but since they were broken we should be as absolute masters of this as of our own orders in council.
Matters went along more or less smoothly between the British and Russian governments for a couple of years. In 1924 Mr. Ramsay MacDonald gave a warning to the commissar for foreign affairs in Leningrad that his agents in London should be a little more careful about the manner in which they were carrying on their trade and other activities.
Mr. A'DSHEAD:	Did you say Mr. Ramsay MacDonald gave the warning?

Yes, in 1924. In 1926,
pressure was brought to bear upon the then Conservative government, of which Lord Balfour was the foreign minister, but he refused to break relations with Russia. He admitted that certain activities were carried on by the Russian agents; he questioned the wisdom of having concluded arrangements with the Russian government, but he thought it would be unwise and imprudent on the part of the British government to break off all relations because of the actions of this or that man. But, as the story goes in London, during all that time in Leningrad there was a tug of war between the Standard Oil Company and the Royal Dutch Oil Company -which, in spite of its Dutch name, is a British company headed by Sir Henri Deterding. There had been what is called a "gentleman's agreement" between those companies. As a rule these gentlemen's agreements cover many things which, for the sake of the parties concerned, are better not uncovered. But it came out that the Russian government had, on the side, granted to the Standard Oil Company certain advantages. Thereupon Sir Henri Deterding beseeched Sir William Joynson-Hicks, the Home Secretary -who in London is known among friendis and foes by the familiar name of "Jix"-to take action, upon which the Home Secretary decided to raid the Arcos building in London, against the wise advice of Sir Austen Chamberlain, Foreign Secretary. But the thing being done, and the documents sought not being found, Sir Austen, thanks to the sanctimonious principle of cabinet solidarity,

Foreign Relations-Mr. Bourassa
was obliged to cover the indiscreet but very radical action of his colleague in favour of Sir Henri Deterding; and therefore he had to announce that the British government could no longer continue relations with the Russian government, because the Russian agents in London had been carrying on frightful acts of international dishonesty and discourtesy, organizing spying on the British government, and so forth.
Following this the very clever and active gentleman who heads the Department for Dominion Affairs, Mr. Amery-who, by the way, if the policy recommended on the other side of the house was carried out would be obliged to step out of the British Empire, because he who rules the dominions is not of English blood; he is a Hungarian Jew, but a very clever man-Mr. Amery wrote to Ottawa to inquire what Canada would do in the matter. His despatch dated May 23, 1927, is very interesting reading:
In connection with my telegrams-
Of course, various telegrams had already been sent to keep us au courant.
-as to Anglo-Soviet relations, we are advised that the termination of the Russian trade agreement of 1921 in relation to this country-
England-

would not-[DOT]
I call the attention of the Prime Minister and the house to this point:
-would not, in the absence of intimation that the notes exchanged on July 3, 1922-
That is, the notes which made us a party to the agreement-
-are no longer regarded as governing the relations between Canada and Soviet, necessarily terminate the operation of the agreement as between the Soviet government and the Canadian government.
In other words, the British government was then advised, and it was its opinion, that Canada stood as a separate party in its relations to Russia. Then, further down:
Especially as the Soviet action which has led to the present situation is directed against the institutions of all parts of the British Empire, we should like to suggest for consideration that as regards the retention of Soviet representatives that this is a matter on which uniformity of action by the various members of the commonwealth concerned would present great advantages.
Upon which the Canadian government- speaking through its improper channel of communication, His Excellency-wired back quite properly:
The despatches received-from Mr. Amery- do not indicate that any documents have been found in . the Arcos raid which establish that the official agency in Canada has been a centre of espionage and subversive propaganda. If
any evidence to this effect has been discovered, it is desired to be informed as early as nossible.
Further down, and quite properly again, His Excellency reminds the British minister that under the very agreement to which Canada was a party, if one government had cause to complain, it had to call the attention of the other government to the fact and ask for an explanation. He asked whether any special steps had been taken towards giving the other party an opportunity of furnishing an explanation; upon which Mr. Amery replied:
Such information as was obtained from Arcos raid directly relating to Canada consisted of addresses found in possession of Anton Miller.
We shall see in a moment what these are.
Second question: It is under third paragraph of article XIII of 1921 agreement that action is being taken by His Majesty's government.
In other words, the British government broke relations with Russia on the strength of this provision:
In the event of the infringement by either party at any time of any of the provisions of this agreement or of the conditions referred to in the preamble, the other party shall immediately be free from the obligations of the agreement.
But the same paragraph contained these words:
Nevertheless it is agreed that before taking any action inconsistent with the agreement the aggrieved party

In this case Great Britain-
-shall give the other party-*
In this case Russia-
-a reasonable opportunity of furnishing an explanation or remedying the default.
Now, by agreeing unreservedly to this provision we were bound to pursue a course which Sir William Joynson-Hicks did not think fit to adopt. Strange to say, without waiting for the documents to be submitted-either those that related to Britain or those obscure but famous addresses found in the possession of Anton Miller-and without having in their possession any of the evidence gathered by the police of London-without waiting for any of these documents or for the documents deposited on the table of the British Commons, the Canadian government decided to break the agreement. The reason I do not know, but we have tihis admission dated May 26. I may say that Mr. Amery's letter was dated iMay 23, to which we replied on the 26th:
So far as Canada is concerned there has been a steady and substantial growth of trade under the agreement, and there has not been any substantial ground of complaint as to espionage or propaganda against the present official agent in Canada.

This is an official declaration signed by the Governor General on Canada's behalf. Nevertheless,
My ministers have concluded that the evidences of espionage and subversive propaganda set forth by your prime minister (Mr. Baldwin) make it clear that an essential condition of the agreement as entered into by Canada as well as by Great Britain, namely, that each party should refrain from hostile action, etc., . . . has not been fulfilled. In order to remove any doubt as to whether the agreement lapses automatically and having regard to all the circumstances they have accordingly decided to terminate the agreement.
It appears therefore, that without haying in the'ir possession the whole or any part of the evidence in the matter, and while admitting that they had no ground of complaint against the Russian representative in Canada, the Canadian government broke that agreement upon a mere despatch from Mr. Amery stating that tlhe prime minister had deposited some papers on the table in the British House of Commons.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Very well, Mr. Speaker. This is the amendment:
This house regrets that proper steps have not yet been taken to give full effect, both in domestic and external affairs, to the "equality of status" acknowledged by the Imperial conference, 1926, to be the "root-principle" of the relationship between the self-governing Britannic communities.
The papers came, but they came late. After we had followed suit, upon Mr. Amery's prompt invitation, we find that Mr. Amery wias not in a. hurry to dispatch the papers. The rupture occurred on May 26 and the papers left London by mail on June 10. They arrived here, and all that was found relating to Canada was this:

Then there is a very long list covering all the countries on earth. It ends with the following:

I do not know whether it is due to the influence of Toronto, but strange to say all these bolshevists are to be found in that holy, sanctimonious centre, the Queen City. Now, that is all that concerns Canada in all that record; there is nothing else. With regard to those evidences of which His Excellency the Governor General, speaking in our name, felt quite satisfied that they justified us in breaking the agreement, without reference to the procedure which we had undertaken to follow in such a situation, they also came later on. I will not read them. May I venture to say that before the government had acted without reading them, they should at leas* have read the expressions of opinion giver in the parliament at Westminster? If they were obliged to draw their inspiration from London, it seems to me that a Liberal gov emment might perhaps have borrowed something from the leaders of liberalism in England rather than to take their cue exclusively from Mr. Amery. What did Mr. Lloyd George think of the matter, as leader of the Liberal party in England? I have the British debates here and any hon. member may consult them if he cares to do so. Mr. Lloyd George said in effect:	"Of course you have evidence of espionage; you have evidence of intrigue. But that is exactly what we are doing ourselves in every country; that is what every government has been engaged in, not only during the war, but before and after. Every government employs spies in every other country. We knew that when we entered into relations with Russia. Lord Balfour knew it; and notwithstanding the same propaganda and espionage, or worse, he refused to break relations in 1926." Mr. Pon-sonby, one of the most distinguished members of the Labour party, and, as everyone knows, the scion of a very aristocratic family, related how, in a previous incident, the head of the criminal investigation department in London, Sir Basil Thomson, to make a case against Russia, had forged a document, which Mr. Ponsonby read to the House of Commons. And this was not contradicted. Mr. Arthur Henderson, who had been a member of the coalition government during the war and who was also in the Labour government in 1924-25, related how he himself, a member of His Majesty's government, sitting

Foreign Relations-Mr. Bourassa
in Berne as a delegate of the British government in an international conference, was spied upon by a paid agent of the same British government; and that spy, not receiving his fee quickly enough from the minister of the crown who employed him to spy on one of his colleagues, went to the Swiss government and sold the documents. It was the Bernese police who put into the hands of Mr. Henderson, a minister of the crown, the papers and reports of an English spy employed by the English; government to spy upon another member of that government in a foreign capital.
After these expressions of opinion and statements of the policy pursued by all governments in every country, perhaps we might have waited at least to read the papers and the judgment passed upon them by such distinguished members of the Labour party and the Liberal party before we agreed, on a simple command from Mr. Amery, to break relations with Russia. I do not say that we had no cause to do so; I do not know. However, I find in the record before us that we have broken relations with Russia simply and solely because the British government did so; and that break in London was condemned by some of the most representative men of public Liberal opinion in England as contrary to the interests of England. Now the story is out, although I do not know whether or not it is true, that this was done at the command of a large financial institution in London, quarrelling with a rival American institution for the favour of the Leningrad government.
I have not brought up this matter for the mere pleasure of unearthing disputable proceedings on the part of the British or any other government; in this regard the British government is no worse than any other gov- [DOT] ernment in the world. As Mr. Henderson and Mr. Lloyd George pointed out, in the present state of things, all governments follow these practices; but I have brought this matter up to indicate how important it is, now that we are beginning to establish relations with foreign countries, to be very prudent in concluding those relations, in order to make sure that they are designed to serve those interests which are confided to us. We should confine our engagements to what is commanded by our own position, and should not rely blindly upon statesmen responsible to the people of the United Kingdom, on the other side of the ocean, to prepare and to conclude our relations, and then break them, for reasons which may be good or bad but have no application to Canada.
There is one feature which it is perhaps still more important to keep in mind. In this instance, we broke our relations with a foreign country because of some difficulty arising in London between the British government and the representatives of that foreign country. There is now a representative of the United States of America in Ottawa, and we have a representative of Canada at Washington. Supposing trouble arose to-morrow; supposing the American government found fault with Mr. Massey or whoever might succeed him, and asked us to recall our representative, as once the American government requested the recall of Sir Lionel Sackville-West for some indiscretion in political matters. Are we going to write to London and, for the sake of "unity of action," ask that the American ambassador be expelled from London? The Irish Free State is also represented in Washington, and the United States is represented in Dublin. Supposing trouble arises, as it may, since modern Irishmen take an equal interest in politics to that which they took in the olden days; supposing the representative of the Irish Free State in AVashing-ton should commit some indiscretion such as the representative of the English government committed forty years ago, and the American government asked Dublin to recall their indiscreet representative. Would Mr. Cosgrave, or his successor, write to the Prime Minister here and ask us to expel the American representative from Ottawa, or recall our minister from AVashington, for the sake of "unity of action?" This is an aspect of the situation which should be studied immediately. We should consider seriously whether we are to maintain our relations with these foreign countries regardless of what action is taken in London, or whether we are to break our relations every time there is trouble between London and any of these other countries. I think this is a very important point. It is a source from which may emanate more trouble than we anticipate, if we do not make our position quite clear in the beginning. If our relations are not to stand by themselves; if we are obliged to break relations every time there is trouble between London and Washington, or Tokyo, or Paris, what becomes of our "equality of status?" If it works only one way and never the other I do not see where the equality lies. As I have already said, this is a very important point, and I am quite sure the Prime Minister will take it in the spirit I am bringing it forward, that is, in order to find a happy solution for all concerned.

Foreign Relations-Mr. Bourassa
In contrast to this, let me point out the absurd situation which we had to face, as a nation and as a government, through an unhappy incident which preceded the present session. I refer to the action of the Mexican consul, Mr. Barron. I need not tell the house that I am not going to discuss the religious or any other policy of the Mexican government. I am not concerned with that to-day, although I have my own views about it. It has been said that we should have broken relations with Mexico in a tragic fashion. I do not agree with that, first because as a matter of fact we have no official relations with Mexico. Then again, I am not quite sure that our standard of Christianity as a nation gives us any moral authority to teach lessons to all nations on earth. Again, it must be admitted, gladly or sadly, that for many centuries past religion and morality have ceased to have any connection with international relations, and it would have been ludicrous for the Canadian government to break relations with Mexico on account of its religious policy when, at about the same time, we were establishing official relations with the government of France. The Mexican policy is more brutal; but if it is a question of Christianity, I think if any modern government on earth has worked effectively for half a century to destroy Christianity, it is the government of the French republic. But there is a further reason. When we see that the Holy See itself is entering into relations, when the opportunity affords, with all governments, Catholic, Protestant, pagan or unfaithful, I do not think it behooves us to be more Catholic than the Pope and to establish or break relations in international affairs on the basis of religion.
But when it comes to the personal attitude of Mr. Barron, that is a different question. This gentleman chose to make use of the Canadian press to insult a bishop of Canada, a Canadian citizen, and then to insult a member of this house, another Canadian citizen. In every other country on earth, including the Black republic of Liberia, that gentleman would have been invited to leave within twenty-four hours. Sir Lionel Sack-ville-West, the ambassador of the great British nation, was asked to leave the United States for an indiscretion of much less magnitude than that committed by Mr. Barron, and this without any protest on the part of the British government.
It has 'been suggested that the Canadian government could do nothing because Mr. Barron was not accredited to the Canadian

government, but to the British government. A certain Mr. Aiken, consul ad bonorem of the republic of Venezuela, gave his opinion on this great question to the Montreal Gazette. He said that the Canadian government couiki take no action because Mr. Barron, as well as himself and other consuls, was not accredited to the Canadian government but to the British government. He was then asked this question, "But what about the last Imperial conference?" and he replied, "The last Imperial conference had nothing to do with that. In that respect Canada is still a .cottony." I Should like to know from the Prime Minister, who has in such glowing terms and eloquent language extolled the glorious position which this country occupies since the last Imperial conference, whether or not it is the Canadian government that is right, or whether it is Mr. Barron or Mr. Aiken. I should like to know whether or not foreign consuls in this country are to be allowed to commit indiscretions, breaches of etiquette and of international rules, which they would not be allowed to commit in Hayti or in the republic of Liberia. Not that I have any poor opinion of the niggers; but, to come back to the comparison I used once, I am afraid that the quality niggers of Canada have a little less pride than the less sophisticated negroes of these republics.
H we want to give full force to what was decided at the last Imperial conference, means should be taken to have all foreign consuls accredited to the Dominion government, and they should receive their approval from this government and not from London. If we want to avoid such misunderstandings, if we want to avoid the ridiculous position we were placed in in this instance, I think we should insist-it would be a very easy matter to settle-that these foreign consuls should be accredited to us, just as they are accredited to the Irish government in the Irish Free State, and to South Africa and so forth.
