speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
After the thoughtful, comprehensive and convincing speech to which we have listened, I fancy very little remains to be said. However, I should like to associate myself with the motion that has been proposed, as I regard it as of very far-reaching importance. The form of the motion has been explained by the mover. I am frank to say that although I wish the government to travel a bit faster and to take a more courageous course along this line I have no more confidence-perhaps I might say, a little less confidence-in the Conservative party in regard to international affairs.
It is rather remarkable that these questions of our foreign relations should create so little interest in Canada. We are interested in post offices in the maritimes or in harbours in Quebec; we become tremendously excited about the tariff. But in these questions, which are of importance to every Canadian, it seems as if comparatively few members take any vital interest. I need only remind the house that approximately one-half of our total revenue goes to pay the interest on the last war. That in itself should indicate the necessity of placing our international relations on some better footing than has been the case in the past. I know that not merely in Canada, but even in the old land, it has not been very customary to have foreign affaire freely discussed by the rank and file in parliament.
Did my hon. friend say that one-half of our revenues went to pay the interest on the war?
Practically one-half.
If the hon. gentleman had Said one-third he would have been nearer the fact.

If the hon. gentleman would take the trouble to consult a speech I made a little earlier in the session, in which I took >as the basis the statement of the Minister of Finance!, and added certain other figures which properly should be charged-increased cost of collection of debts, and so forth-he would find that I am well within the mark. As I was saying, it has not been very customary for the rank and file to discuss foreign affairs; but now that we in Canada are brought so closely in touch with various other countries it is important that we should form the habit in this parliament of discussing, more fully than we have done heretofore, those questions which relate to our external affairs.

Several years .ago we set up a committee on industrial and international relations. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself suggested that international relations should come under the supervision of that committee, but so far not one question of international relationships has been referred to it. I would urge upon the Prime Minister that next year some of these questions be brought before this committee in order that we may discuss them in greater detail than can be done in the house.
I wish to state in a very brief form my own opinion with regard to the question before the house. First of all Canada's views on imperial policy or international affairs are not necessarily those of Great Britain. That,
I think, has been well illustrated by the last speaker. Secondly, opinions on these matters differ widely in Great Britain. We all' know thlat there is a Conservative policy, there is a Liberal policy and there is a Labour policy in Great Britain. Why should we always take the point of view of the Baldwin government? I hope within a very dhort time to see the Labour party in power in Great Britain. When that takes place I trust I shall have the great satisfaction of urging my friends in this house to follow the lead of the motherland.
Why any more than any other?

Not more than any of the others, of course. But since my Conservative friends are continually telling us when the Baldwin government is in power, that we ought to follow the motherland, they would be only consistent in following the motherland even when the Labour party is in power. As for me, I would say that we ought to choose our own policy whether the Baldwin government or a Labour government be in power in Great Britain.
In this country we so rarely read anything in regard to the policies of the opposition parties in Great Britain that I venture to quote from The Spectator, a quite respectable English paper which I think ought to appeal to the present government. This paper, in the issue of January 28, 1928, gives a summary of certain observations of His Majesty's government in Great Britain on the suggested program of work of the subcommittee on security of the Preparatory Commission on Disarmament which, states this journal:
-constitutes a document of considerable importance, for it embodies a full statement of the considered views of the British government on the questions, first of arbitration, and secondly of security agreements.

Foreign Relations-Mr. Woodsworth
I will not stop to read the summary but I wish to quote the Spectator's comment:
_ This statement of policy must be read in its relation to disarmament on the one hand and security on the other. The doctrine gaining increasing ground on the continent of Europe is that for disarmament to become a practical proposition it is necessary to arrange for the peaceful settlement of all international disputes, not merely of some. That means submitting all such disputes to some form of pacific settlement, legal or justiciable cases normally going to the Permanent Court and non-justici-abJe cases being settled by arbitration, if conciliation fails. The British memorandum, it will be observed, assents to neither part of this proposition, and Great Britain still declines to undertake to have legal disputes settled by the co]rrt or non-legal disputes by arbitration.
With regard to legal cases, Lord Pbillimore has recently stated convincingly in the Spectator the case for sending all such questions as a matter of course to the Permanent Court. Twenty-eight nations have so far signed the optional clause, whereby they undertake to do this, and, though ratification is still required m some cases, the clause at present binds twenty states. Germany and France both have bills providing for ratification before their respective parliaments.
If twenty-eight states are willing to sign the optional clause why should not Canada sign it? The trouble is, we have bound ourselves at the Imperial conference to take no action without first consulting the motherland. I think we should at once represent to the motherland the advisability of our signing the optional clause. However, let me proceed with this statement:
With regard to non-justiciable disputes, it is to be observed that Great Britain appears to have gone back on the policy she supported at Locarno, for she there applauded France and Germany in their decision "to settle by peaceful means all questions of every kind which may arise between them," whereas the British note declares that there are some political questions, even of a justiciable nature, which a state cannot agree unreservedly in advance to submit to arbitration. Elsewhere it is stated that nonjusticiable disputes are unsuitable for submission to a tribunal capable of giving a binding decision. These objections, which appear-if they have any meaning at all-to leave the door open for war in the last resort, are equally difficult to reconcile with the resolution unanimously carried with the specific approval of Great Britain at the last League assembly, declaring "that every pacific means must be employed to settle disputes of every description which may arise between states."
It would seem, Mr. Speaker, that the real trouble with regard to the optional clause lies in Great Britain's traditional policy of sea power in time of war, and I fancy that in Canada, sooner or later, we will have to face the question of whether or not we propose to stand by Great Britain's position in this regard. I think very few people realize
56103-219J
that Great Britain has not receded from the position of one hundred years ago. I would like to quote a few passages with regard to the Stigstad case, which was before the Privy Council, and which I think well illustrates what I would regard as the perfectly indefensible position of Great Britain in this regard. This was an appeal from the prize court of England. A neutral ship on her way to Rotterdam with goods destined for Germany was required to discharge at a British port; no unreasonable delay or expense in carrying out the provision of the order was incurred. It was held, that the order in council did not entail unreasonable inconvenience on neutrals and was valid, and that the neutral shipowner was not entitled to damages for the detention of the ship or to expenses.
I quote from the argument on which this decision was based, page 285 of the English law reports, appeal cases, 1919:
What is here in question is not the right of the belligerent to retaliate upon his enemy the same measure as has been meted out to him, or the propriety of justifiing in one belligerent some departure from the regular rules of war on the ground of necessity arising from prior departures on the part of the other, but it is the claim of neutrals to be saved harmless under such circumstances from inconvenience or damage thereout arising.
And again:
-the only question open to the neutral claimant for the purpose of invalidating the order is whether or not it subjects neutrals to more inconvenience or prejudice than is reasonably necessary under the circumstances.
And again:
_ In considering whether more inconvenience is inflicted upon neutrals than the circumstances involve, the frequency and the enormity of the original wrongs are alike material, for the more gross and universal those wrongs are, the more are all nations concerned in their repression, and bound for their part to submit to such sacrifices as that repression involves. It is right to recall that, as neutral commerce suffered and was doomed to suffer gross prejudice from the illegal policy proclaimed and acted on by the German government, so it profited by, and obtained relief from, retaliatory measures, if effective to restrain, to punish and to bring to an end such injurious conduct. Neutrals, whose principles or policy lead them to refrain from punitory or repressive action of their own, may well be called on to bear a passive part in the necessary suppression of courses which are fatal to the freedom of all who use the seas.
And a little later on:
The assumption was that a neutral, too pacific or too impotent to resent the aggressions and lawlessness of one belligerent, can require the other to refrain from his most effective, or his only, defence against it, by the assertion of an
3460	COMMONS
Foreign Relations-Mr. Woodworth.
absolute inviolability for his own neutral trade, which would thereby become _ engaged in a passive complicity with the original offender. For this contention no authority at all was forthcoming.
I ask whether any member of this house would subscribe to this doctrine:
The seas are the highway of all, and it is incidental to the very nature of maritime war that neutrals, in using that highway, may suffer inconvenience from the exercise of their concurrent rights by those who have to wage war upon it.
Surely it is an altogether new doctrine that the warring people have the rights while the neutral people have no rights, or only partial rights. I proceed:
.... to say that retaliation is invalid as against neutrals, except within the old limits of blockade, contraband, and unneutral service, is to reduce retaliation to a mere simulacrum, the title of an admitted right without practical application or effect.
That is still the position of Great Britain. Let me contrast that with the attitude of the United States, our great neighbour to the south, who will not and need not tolerate very much longer the unwarrantable position taken by Great Britain. I would like to quote a few passages from a recent article appearing in the Contemporary Review for April, 1928. by Colonel Edward M. House, who says:
The failure of the Geneva naval conference has emphasized the difficulties of reaching an understanding regarding the relative strength of armaments. A simple and far more effective way out vrould be for the sea powers to agree to a code of sea laws making battleships of all kinds useless except for defensive purposes. The only adequate means by which this may be accomplished is through an agreement to accept the principle of the freedonr of the seas in so far as it means the abolition of contraband and immunity of private property at sea.
He refers to the second Hague conference of 1907, when an American proposal was presented urging the immunity of private property, of neutral and belligerent alike, from seizure at sea, and also a British proposal urging the abondonment of the principle of contraband altogether. Lord Reay, stating the case for the British proposal, said:
Recent experience, gentlemen, has therefore confirmed my government in its opinion. It remains firmly convinced that in the present condition of world commerce and of human knowledge the exercise of the right of seizure results only in hampering neutral commerce without giving belligerents compensating advantages and in bringing the former eventually into the war. It is, therefore, with the firm conviction that the time has come to remove the dangers which I have pointed out, that the British delegation has the honour to propose that contraband be abolished and that neutral commerce be restored to the freedom which it requires.
[Mr. Woodsworth.l
Then Mr. House comments on that statement, and says:
The British were absolutely right in abandoning the principle of contraband. No halfway measure will suffice. There can be no longer a distinction between articles destined for military purposes and those intended for the civilian population. On the other hand, until private property on the high seas is made immune, the troublesome and dangerous differences of opinion that arose in 1812 and 1915 are bound to return in the ease of another war. What is suggested, then, is simply the acceptance of the British proposal of 1907 for the abolition of contraband and of the American proposal of the same year for the sanctity of private property at sea.
He quotes Commander Kenworthy as having stated in an article in the London Review of Reviews:
The one nation that can be successful^ blockaded is Britain, and yet we cling to the weapon which may possibly bring about our destruction.
And he concludes:
With the freedom of the seas guaranteed by covenant between nations, there would be no incentive for the United States, I ranee, Germany or Russia or other powers to maintain navies larger than sufficient for ponce purposes.
And again:
The benefits which would accrue to Great Britain through the freedom of the seas would be free communication with her dominions, and the certainty that her food supply and raw materials could never be interrupted, buch a policy would eliminate the terrors of submarine warfare, for submarine could be used only against battleships and craft of war.
I do not think I could better summarize the position of some of the most thoughtful English Liberals and Labour leaders with regard to this question of the blockade than by quoting from a recent speech by Mr. W. Arnold-Forster. He says:
(a)	The blockade weapon is no longer divisible. It is impossible to distinguish between civil, medical, and military stores.
(b)	It is more generally detested than ever. Europe remembers that 760,000 died in consequence of England's blockade before the armistice and 100,000 during its continuance afterwards; that the Russian famine resulted largely in consequence of the stoppage of farming machinery; that supplies were refused to Greek islands which favoured Constantine; and that for the year 1917-18 even the neutral nation Sweden received no supplies. And America remembers our interference with her shipping, and the 12,000 tons of her copper which were piled up on the mole at Gibraltar.
(e) It is now much more impracticable. In 1914 there were only two cables between Germany and America, one of which we cut, and the other we diverted and tapped. And the prize courts showed the value of the information which came from that source. Now there are many means of communicating the movements of ships, both under the sea and above it.

Foreign Relations-Mr. Woodsworth
(d) It follows that it is now less defensible as a weapon, from all points of view. We must, of course, remember that the United States is outside the League of Nations, and might decide to help a nation which had disobeyed the league. But if we renounce the blockade we shall be in a position to ask that the United States of America on her part will not assist a proven aggressor.
I am quoting at length to-day for a set purpose. If on my own authority I made these Statements they might be challenged by members of this house as being merely my own personal opinion, or as representing the opinion of one small group in this house. I would point out that these are the views of very large and influential groups of people in Great Britain. I will quote the position of the Liberals in Great Britain, and I wonder if the Canadian government will go as far as the Liberals in Great Britain are willing to go. They demand that the British government should at once take the following measures:
1.	To sign the undertaking framed by the League of Nations, to refer all international disputes of a legal character to the league's court of justice at The Hague.
2.	To enter into general or particular treaties of arbitration providing for the peaceful settlement of other disputes.
3.	To reduce our own existing armaments, which are beyond the needs of the present situation, and specifically to repudiate any policy of entering into a competition in naval construction with the United States of America.
4.	To press forward the action which is contemplated for codifying and defining more closely the principles of international law.
The Liberal memorial states:
In our judgment the failure of Great Britain to retain the foremost place in the world movement towards a more rational and a more moral civilization is due in material part to the hesitating action and divided counsels of the government.
This is not a statement made by some irresponsible group, but is the formal statement of the Liberal party of Great Britain.
I would also appeal to my Conservative friends to be as broadminded and as far-seeing as some of the leading Conservatives in Great Britain. About the time the Liberals were taking the position they did, the general council of the League of Nation's Union, upon motion of Lord Robert Cecil, put out a declaration urging upon the government a programme of co-operation with the league under five heads, the second being in these terms:
2. To promote the peaceful settlement of all international disputes by every means in its power, and with this object immediately,

(a)	To sign the optional clause with any reservations that may be necessary to provide for the special position of this country.
(b)	To announce its willingness to negotiate all-inclusive arbitration agreements with any civilized nation, on a model to be established by the League of Nations.
I would ask the Prime Minister why we should not proceed immediately to negotiate with the British government with a view to securing our release from our present obligations and enabling us to sign at once the optional clause.
Further since the Root treaty of 1908 has now expired, I would ask why a treaty cannot be made between Canada and the United States which will be much more inclusive in its character than that which is now being proposed by Mr. Kellogg. If I understand the situation aright, Great Britain is putting in so many reservations that the treaty will be comparatively useless, or at least will stop very far short of what we in this country want. Why should we not proceed at once to renew our treaty with the United States, renew it in the name of His Majesty on behalf of Canada, and make it without any reservations-an all-inclusive arbitration treaty?
Does my hon. friend suggest that the treaty forwarded to Canada by the United States is not the treaty without any reservations or without the reservations put in by Sir Austen Chamberlain?

I will leave that
to the Prime Minister to answer. I would hope that it was the original treaty as put forward by Mr. Kellogg and not the treaty as emasculated by the interpretations of the present administration in Great Britain.
I want to follow the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) for a few minutes in his references to Russia. It may be comparatively safe for the member for Labelle to refer to Russia, but I suppose it is much more dangerous for me to do so because of the general popular conception that the Labour movement is seriously affected with sympathy for Russia. We are sympathetic with Russia; I do not deny it. I regard the experiment in Russia as one of the greatest that has been made in any part of the world, or in any age in history. We can look back to-day with something like a dispassionate view to the achievements of the French revolution, and I believe the time is coming when we will look back to the Russian revolu-
3462	COMMONS
Foreign Relations-Mr. Woodsworth
tion of ten years ago as marking one of the greatest epochs in the history of the world. I am not suggesting that we in Canada should proceed along Russian lines-that is another question.
The trouble is that we have been prejudiced by our newspapers against Russia. Instead of quoting some socialist or labour authority, I would like to quote, in opening up this discussion, a few words from our good friend Colonel H. J. Mackie. Colonel Mackie has spent a good many years in Russia; he was head of the Canadian section of the movement which attempted to relieve the children of Russia some years ago. Colonel Mackie, who I believe is regarded as a good Conservative, was quoted by the Toronto Daily Star of February 2, 1927 as follows:
''The chief obstacle in the way of friendly relations between Great Britain and Russia is the wilful, stupid hostility and misrepresentation of British politicians, particularly Churchill, Birkenhead and Joynson-Hicks", declared Col. Herbert J. Mackie, former M.P. for North Renfrew, who, since 1920, has been in Russia ten different times. He has just recently returned from his latest visit.
Colonel Mackie continues:
The situation in Russia to-day is simply unbelievable to anyone who has the picture of the Russia of 1920 in his mind.
To the external view the people one sees on '*the streets of Moscow and Leningrad are well [DOT]dressed, happy, contented and prosperous.
Wonderful strides are being made in education. The commissar of education told me that he was much interested in the Canadian rural school system and that he hoped to send a commission of five educationists to Canada next spring to study our methods.
Again:
I have been greatly impressed with the absolute sincerity of the men at the top of Russian affairs.
"Stalin is the great man of Russia to-day," said Col. Mackie.
He is a quiet, reserved man, but he is very able, and the people trust him.
Trotsky's power is on the wane.
One thing that has impressed me greatly in Russia is that the leaders there are willing to admit their mistakes and to change their plans if they find they will not work.

What happened to
Trotsky?

I think we all know that Trotsky was banished. For the few minutes that remain to me I should like to speak of our relationship with this Soviet Russia, which is apparently not nearly so black a country as many have painted it. I would refer hon. members to a very interesting article on Russia in Toronto Saturday

Night on March 24 of this year. An hon. member suggests that this is a socialist paper. I think I am comparatively safe in quoting Toronto Saturday Night.

No, the hon. member is
not. It is not a safe paper.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I assume, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members who wish to take part in this debate have spoken, because I would have preferred to wait before replying until all the members who have any intention of speak-
3464	COMMONS
Foreign Relations-Mr. Mackenzie King
ing have spoken, as I would like in my remarks to cover whatever points may be raised by the different speakers.
May I remind the house that the motion before it at the moment is that the house go into committee of supply, the supply being that of the Department of External Affairs. I refer particularly to this because my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), who has moved an amendment, has mentioned that one of his reasons for his so doing was that in that manner only was it possible for him to address the house on the various subjects to which he has referred. I might say to my hon. friend that I think he would have had that opportunity the minute we got into supply, with respect to the different items that would come before the committee. However, I recognize he might not have had it in a manner which would1 have afforded him the opportunity of reviewing in the comprehensive and logical way he has done the different subjects referred to in the course of his remarks.
I should like to read the amendment anew. It is as follows:
This house regrets that proper steps have not yet been taken to give full effect, both in domestic and external affairs, to the "equality of status" asknowledged by the Imperial conference, 1926, to be the "root-principle" of the relationship between the self-governing Britannic communities.
That amendment has this merit in particular, that it approves in no uncertain tone the formula which was laid down at the Imperial conference with respect to the position of Canada and the other self-governing dominions and the British government. The equality of status which is there set forth is the root principle of the relationship.
I may say that on the whole, my hon. friend's remarks in relation to the government were quite as appreciative as they were critical of its attitude in dealing with matters pertaining to Canada's external affairs, and I am sure that I am not far off the mark when I say that I do not think my hon. friend desires his amendment to be considered as a motion of want of confidence in the administration. I hope that when I have endeavoured to reply to what he has said, he will feel that his purpose has been served in bringing before the house and the country the various matters he has, and that it will not be necessary to press the amendment to a division; for certainly were that to be done, the government would be obliged to ask the house to vote against the amendment. With the exception of the one word "regrets," which appears in it, and the delay alleged, I for my part would

be rather prepared, under other circumstances, to accept a resolution along the lines of the purport and purpose my hon. friend has in mind. The purport and purpose of the resolution is simply that, as opportunity arises, the government should do what lies in its power, to carry out the principles laid down at the last Imperial conference, establishing Canada's position as one of the British dominions, on an equality so far as status is concerned, with that of Great Britain. With respect therefore to the real purport of the resolution there is no exception to be taken on the part of the administration, and as I have already said, I hope that my hon. friend will later on feel in regard to the matters he has brought up that perhaps he has seen them from an angle which has not afforded him the full light which he should have had in moving a resolution critical of the administration.
The first point that my hon. friend dealt with was the manner in which communications were being carried on between the government of Canada and the British government. He drew attention to the fact that at the Imperial conference of 1926 it was decided that thereafter communications passing between His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in Great Britain should be direct as from government to government, and not through the channel existing at the time, namely, the office of His Excellency the Governor General. My hon. friend said that he was somewhat surprised in looking at the correspondence relating to the severance of relations with Russia to discover that though that correspondence took place in May, His Excellency the Governor General was still the medium of communication, and that the Canadian government was not communicating direct with the government of Great Britain. May I say to my hon. friend that in all these matters of changed relations, if they are to be described as such, the line of evolution, rather than of revolution, is in the long run almost certain to be the most effective one and the most enduring, and a change, even when it is a desirable one, is sometimes carried out to the better satisfaction of all concerned where time is taken to see that all interested parties are fully apprised of the significance of the change, and that all the necessities in relation thereto are properly met. My hon. friend will realize that for the Department of External Affairs to take over the work of conducting the direct communication with England, as it was being done through the

Foreign Relations-Mr. Mackenzie King
office of His Excellency the Governor General, there was need, for that purpose, of an appropriation by this parliament to the Department of External Affairs. The conference met in London in November; the estimates which were brought to parliament for the current year contained an appropriation which would enable the Department of External Affairs to take over the communications. It was necessary to add to the staff of the department for purposes of coding and transcribing despatches, and to have therefor, as well as for the cost of transmission, extra appropriations. Parliament had only voted the appropriation at the time the correspondence took place with regard to our relations with Russia. That of itself, as I think my hon. friend will recognize, was a sufficient reason why the change should not have been made abruptly or immediately after the conference had registered its decision with respect to it. On the other hand, there was the further circumstance that the British government's wishes had also to be considered. It was to some extent a matter as between the British government and all the dominions with respect to the form this particular change would take and the time when it would be made. We were led to believe that it was desirable to give the foreign office and the dominions office time to perfect the necessary changes in their departments, and that was another reason why there was no immediate action taken in changing the channel of communication.
However, I might say to my hon. friends that there was still a further reason. When the estimates were introduced it would be the beginning of the fiscal year, and the change, I presume, might have been made then on the assumption that parliament would support the administration. But, all things considered, it seemed to us that the first of July last year, being Dominion Day and of particular significance in that it marked the diamond jubilee of confederation, would be an appropriate date on which to bring this change into effect. Therefore early in the year we suggested to His Majesty is government in Great Britain that we hoped, so far as they were concerned, matters would not be delayed beyond the first of July. That date was regarded as quite acceptable to the British government, and on the first of July the communications between His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in Great Britain began to be exchanged direct, and have continued from that moment to be so exchanged. My hon. friend may now fee1! assured that the change about which he was so anxious was made nearly a year ago. Many of the communications which now for nearly a year
have been exchanged direct between the two governments are between prime minister and prime minister; some of them are sent direct to the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs in London; but for convenience sake, and also for it-he sake of record, all communications in the first instance come to our government through the office of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and communications to the British government go through the office of the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs in London. Let me say that from the moment the arrangement was introduced up to the present it has worked admirably and I think to the distinct advantage of both governments. I do not wish to make comparisons with the length of time previously taken, but certainly there has been to some extent a lessening of the time required through the elimination of the roundabout process which formerly was in vogue.
My hon. friend spoke next of the particular paragraph in the report of the Imperial conference which sets forth that matters relating to the operation of dominion legislation should be referred to a special committee, and he took exception to the fact that up to the present time that committee has apparently not been formed.
Mr. BOURASS0A: If ,the right hon. gentleman will allow me? I put it in the form of a question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad to accept my hon. friend's correction. I apologize to him for having used the term "book exception." My hon. friend asked: Has the committee been formed; if not, when is it to be formed? When the Secretary of State for the Dominions, the Right Hon. Mr. Amery, was in Ottawa at the beginning of this session, I spoke to him concerning the convening of the committee. Mr. Amery had been in touch with the other dominions in the course of his tour, and he told me that they had all to some extent 'brought up the subject with him, or he had brought it up with them, and after his return home he expected to be in a position formally to communicate with all the dominions as to the formation of tne committee. In other words,
I gathered that he had ascertained from the several dominions their wishes, and was intending to have a communication sent out which would enable the committee to be formed forthwith. Up tO' the present time we have not received a formal communication.
I might say that as a result of this discussion to-day I shall have pleasure in drawing the attention of the Secretary of State for the Dominions to the fact that hon. members think there should not be any further delay
3466	COMMONS
Foreign Relatione-Mr. Mackenzie King
in the establishment of the committee. But may I say this? I do not think there has been any intentional delay on the part of the Secretary of State for the Dominions. I have no doubt that -what has been happening here has been happening aJlso in Great Britain and the other dominions, namely, that the departmental officials have been engaged on what might be considered the statement of the case from the point of view of their respective governments with respect to the several matters to be considered so as to be in a position the minute the committee is called together to make a presentation of the case. As to Canada, some of the officers of the Department of External Affairs and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) with the officers of his department have been conferring together and studying certain aspects of the question. Similarly, in the Department of Marine and Fisheries there have been- experts at work on different phases of the question relating to merchant shipping, which is also to be dealt with by means of a committee. I think my hon. friend may feel assured that the committee will be called very shortly, and that the position of Canada or of any other part of the empire will not be prejudiced by the delay.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, whatever work these committees perform will likely come before the next Imperial conference, and I presume their report will be made to that conference. Just when the conference will be 'held I cannot say at the moment, but in the natural order of things it would not be before the fall of next year. I think, therefore, there is plenty of time for the committee to meet and make its report.
I was pleased to see that my hon. friend approved so whole-heartedly of the intention of the government to establish legations in Paris and Tokyo, and also of the step already taken in establishing a legation at Washington. With respect to the word of counsel and advice he gave to the administration to proceed in a modest way, may I assure him that we are entirely in accord with him in that particular. There is an old saying which comes to one's mind with respect to these legations, it is that in Rome one must do more or less as the Romans do; and no doubt my hon. friend had in his thoughts the expenses of the legation at Washington. Quite frankly I may say that they are on a scale which the government does not contemplate with regard either to Paris or to Tokyo. But, as he knows, Washington is generally conceded to
[Mr Mackenzie King.]
be the most expensive capital in the world. Even the legation which Canada has is small compared to some of the legations of other countries of very much less importance than our Dominion. What we have done at Washington has been done appropriately, having regard to Canada's relationship to the United States; and I think my hon. friend will be pleased when he sees how Canada's action at Washington will be reciprocated by the United States in its legation here at Ottawa. It is an open secret that the United States government contemplates erecting very shortly in this capital an important and, I may say, an imposing building for the purposes of its legation. As Canadians we shall, I believe, feel proud of what will be done in that regard by the country to the south.
As to the importance of the representation being clearly defined, I agree absolutely with my hon. friend that- it is essential that the position of Canada's minister at any of the capitals in -which there may be legations should be perfectly clear, both as respects his relations with the British minister at that capital and as well, in regard to his relations with the country to which both are accredited.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I had been touching upon the representation of Canada in legations abroad and the position of ^ our representatives in relation to the other British representatives and also in relation to the representatives of the countries to which they are accredited. The hon. member who moved the amendment stressed the importance of these relations being Clearly defined. Naturally I entirely agree with him in that; personally I see very little difficulty in the definition. The representatives of Canada to other countries are appointed in reference to the domestic and external affairs of Canada, and they 'have to deal only with matters in respect of which we are primarily concerned. At these legations they meet, in the same capitals, the representatives of the British government who are similarly charged with the responsibility of representing the British government in regard to its domestic and foreign affairs, wherever those domestic and foreign affairs come to be a matter of international interest and concern. It is conceivable that in some cases the foreign affairs of one part of the empire will intersect the arc which relates to the foreign affairs of

Foreign Relations-Mr. Mackenzie King
another part of the empire. In that event one would assume that the obligation with reference to what is held in common would be a joint obligation and that the two represents atives, or more if there are such, would carry out their trusteeship in eo-operation with each other after consultation. Possibly there may be some who will object that there is always the possibility of difference arising. That possibility exists everywhere and if it is to come up between representatives of different parts of the empire perhaps it is fortunate that it should arise first of all between two individuals, and subsequently be referred to their respective governments, by whom any difference could be smoothed out, as differences have been dealt with in the course of years where they have arisen between different governments of the same empire, I believe that is all I need to say with reference to the position of our representatives abroad.
The next subject mentioned by the hon, member for Labelle was the action of the Dominion government in severing relations with Russia. That action was taken just a year ago this month, about the time or rather at the time the British government severed its relations with Russia. As the hon. member said, the agreement which we had with Russia was one which originated between His Majesty's government of Great Britain and the Union of Soviet Socialistic republics in Russia. That agreement came into being under a (previous administration; Canada's adherence to that agreement was given under that former administration. When we came into office we found that agreement in existence; both governments were parties to it. and naturally we accepted the obligations which arose under it. I think there was an exchange of notes, six months after we came into office, accepting or rather confirming a formula which had been agreed to prior to the time we assumed office.

May I ask a question? Is not the right hon. gentleman in error in stating that the agreement had been confirmed before Mr. Meighen's government was defeated? My memory is that there was no formal agreement until after my right hon. friend came into power, although I speak subject to correction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What I am
now saying is that an .order in council had been passed, first of all, asking the British government if they would ascertain from Russia whether Canada might not become a party to the agreement. Then, after having taken that action, a formula was drafted which
was submitted to or by the British government, and they or our government were asked whether that formula would be acceptable and also if it would be acceptable to the Russian government in order to make Canada a party to the agreement. That formula was approved by an order in council passed by a previous administration, and the British and Russian governments were both advised that Canada would adhere to the treaty under that particular formula. Then, as I recall it, in the following August our administration received a communication from Lord Balfour, who was acting Foreign Minister at the time, stating that the formula had been formally signed.
That was in August of 1922.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is correct, but that was merely carrying out the obligation, in the matter of signature, to which the previous administration had committed the government of Canada. However, that is a mere detail; the facts are that we continued to be bound by the terms of the treaty with Russia, and we received in Canada in 1923 what was known as the Russian trade mission or agency. Russia sent to this country a trade agent, who opened an office in Montreal with a small staff of employees and undertook obligations or duties relating in part to trade and duties in part of a consular character.
I might say to the house that that particular office did not have a very happy beginning as far as the government of Canada was concerned. At the time the Russian agent came to Canada he brought with him what seemed to members of our administration an unnecessary amount of literature of the character of propaganda of communist ideas. So much of this material was brought in that the government found it necessary to question the head of the agency as to its character. Some of the material was brought to Ottawa and ' examined, and I personally saw a good deal of it. It was not the kind of literature which I think should have been brought into this country ,and I very frankly told the Russian agent that that was my opinion of it. I sought to obtain from him reasons as to Why this literature was being brought into Canada, and I obtained answers which were far from satisfactory, so far as my own feelings were concerned, and I think I was inclined to be generous in the attitude I took toward him.

In what language was
this material printed?
_ Mr. MACKENZIE KING: It was printed in different languages. Some of it was tran-
Foreign

Relations-Mr. Mackenzie King
slated and the government went to particular pains to ascertain the nature of the propaganda. Some of it was in the nature of posters which children of any age, whether or not they could read or write, could understand. They were of a character which I do not think any hon. member of tins house would wish to see exhibited about this country.
May I ask if any of the literature was in English?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I drew the
attention of the agent to these posters and asked him whether he thought they were the kind of thing that should be brought into this country, and he admitted quite frankly that if they had not been brought in for the purpose of wrapping he did not think they would have been brought in at all.
My right hon. friend is referring to pictorial posters, not printed ones?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Will the Prime Minister
give us an idea of horv much of this literature was brought in at that time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say how much, but I know sixteen boxes were brought in when the agent arrived.
What was the size of the boxes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They were so large tha-t the only explanation that could be given of them was that their contents were intended as a library or to be used as exchanges with other libraries of this country. Some of the literature attacked religion; some was an attack upon organized economic society, and generally speaking, the literature that I saw was not of the character that I believe my hon. friend would have wished to see circulating in this country. The extraordinary thing about it was that this particular material should have been brought in by an organization whose purpose was the friendly one of the development of trade between this country and Russia.
There were other matters, which I think I may be excused from mentioning at the moment, which gave rise to considerable suspicion in the minds of the administration, so much so that the government contemplated at one time making a search of the quarters in Montreal where this mission was located. This was some time previous to the announcement in the British house that relations had been broken off with Russia, on the part of the
[Mr Mackenzie King.]
British government. Then one day we were advised that the British government had broken off relations, for reasons already mentioned. We had in our possession a statement made by the Prime Minister of Great Britain to the British House of Commons. In addition to that we had the information concerning which there was no question about the circulation of communist propaganda in China by one of the agents of the Russian government. This was contrary to the obligations entered into by Russia in the treaty, and we felt that everything considered we had more than sufficient ground at the time for severing relations with the Russian government. We took prompt action in the matter; we did not wait until the British government had communicated its view of the situation to parliament, we acted before that.
The criticism that has been directed against the government has been that we merely followed the British government. The hon. member for Labelle drew attention to what was in the communication from the Secretary of State for the Dominions, to the effect that unified action on the part of the British Empire would be helpful at that stage. He argued that it was because of that communication and request from the British government that our action was taken. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth), who seconded the amendment, also stressed the point that w.a should have waited to see what was said by Liberal and Labour members in the British parliament. It was precisely because we wished our action to be understood as independent action that we did not wait until discussion had taken place in the British parliament. The criticism of my hon. friend is directed towards us for following the British government, and then he says we should have waited to follow the British parliament. We were not following anyone, we were acting on our own initiative and taking action towards this particular trade mission which we felt was justified in the light of circumstances as we knew them to exist. We did not hesitate to make it known to the officers of the original mission that we were not satisfied with its personnel, and these officers were changed some little time prior to the breaking off of the relations with Russia under the treaty. The agent who was here at that time appeared to me to be a thoroughly honest and honourable man. I had no reason to mistrust him in any particular, and I said so at the time we broke off relations. I am sorry that I can not say the same with respect to his predecessors in office.

Foreign Relations-Mr. Mackenzie King
I would point out to the house the position in which this country would have been placed had the government's action at the time not been wha't it was. Up to the present time the United States has never made a treaty with the Union of Soviet Socialistic republics in Russia. At that time Great Britain had severed connections with Russia in the matter of trade, and this country would have been left as the one part of 'the English speaking world whidh had maintained relations. It seems to me that we would have been put in a position where the rest of the world might well have demanded what exceptional reasons we found to continue a relationship which was likely to prove embarrassing to the rest of the British Empire.
While our action was taken independently of Great Britain and all other parts of the empire, I am perfectly frank in saying that if it was helpful to any one part of the British Empire in a difficult situation, I am all the more pleased on that account. What I want to make clear is this; the taking of similar action to that of another part of the British Empire does not mean .that our action is necessarily obsequious, a mere imitation, or, above all, that it is in any shape or form yielding to dictation.
Would the Canadian government have broken off relations if the British government had not done so?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If we had had
occasion to go carefully into the evidence that we obtained at that time, I think it is quite possible we would have severed relations. In fact, it was very much against our will that we continued relations as long as we did. We continued them simply because we were anxious to avoid embarrassment to other parts of the empire as well as to ourselves. When the situation became such that to have continued longer would have been taking a course Which would have been very doubtful, as far as Canada was concerned, and embarrassing to other parts of the empire, we had no hesitancy in taking the course we did.

Is the statement that the
Prime Minister is at present giving to the house not rather at variance with the statement he issued after relations were broken off?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, I made it quite clear at the time of breaking off the relations that as regards the then Russian agent, we had no exception to take to any action on his part. I confess to my hon. friend that I did not go into the detail into which I have gone to-night with respect to the grounds which we had prior to that time
for suspecting the work of this particular trade mission. The government did not do so at the time because we were anxious not to say any more than was necessary, and I would not have said as much as I have tonight had it not been that, in view of what has been said in the course of the debate, I have felt it was only fair to hon. members to bring before the house these other factors. We were particularly careful to make it clear that we in no way wished to prejudice dealings in trade between Canada and Russia, rather that we were anxious in every way to have those relations furthered. There is no reason why trade relations should not be developed between Canada and Russia just as speedily, happily and effectively as are trade relations between the United States and Russia at the present time, particularly in view of the circumstances that while Russia has no diplomatic relations with the United States, nevertheless she is trading there. She is free to trade in this country. We will welcome the representatives of Russian firms or any representatives who come to trade with the people of Canada. We are anxious that normal trade relations in all particulars shall be restored between Russia and Canada in any particular in which they have been impeded.
May I add this further fact which perhaps I should have mentioned before? The particular agency which had its office in Montreal was claiming, under the treaty it is quite true, immunities and rights of a character which went much beyond those conceded to any consular agencies of other countries. For example, the right was claimed by means of couriers to bring into the country in sealed bags whatever they wished to bring in of their correspondence; in other words, that the mails of Canada were not to be trusted for communications passing between Russia and its office in Montreal. That was a kind of immunity that we could not see was either desirable or necessary for the purpose of promoting legitimate trade, and the importance that was attached to that kind of thing by the office in Monreal aroused a suspicion which the absence of it might have prevented altogether. That, I think, covers all that I need say at the moment with respect to the severance by Canada of its relations under the trade agreement with the union of soviet socialistic republics.

Does the Prime Minister know of any other diplomatic consulate that brings in political propaganda from the country from which it comes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Will the Prime Minister state what were the words of the other form?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Under the procedure laid down at the Imperial conference, a treaty that was to bind only one part of the British Empire was to be made in the name
of His Majesty's government for that part, and that part was to be specifically named, but if the treaty was intended to bind the whole empire, not just one part, it would still be in the name of His Majesty, but the reference would not be specifically to any particular part. It was the latter form in which the treaty was submitted to us. Then elsewhere Lord Parmoor says:
I have on former occasions asked that papers might be laid showing what were the reasons given. I will not press that to-day, because it is not the particular point with which I am dealing. All I can say is that Mr. Mackenzie King's statement is anything but obscure. It is perfectly straightforward. What he originally stated in the Canadian parliament is correct, that the Anglo-Egyptian treaty was first submitted to the Canadian government in a form which made Canada a party to that treaty.
That statement was made by Lord Parmoor in the House of Lords, and to that the Marquess of Salisbury replied a little later on in the course of the debate. I might read the reference which Lord Salisbury makes in that regard (House of Lords reports, page 894):
In regard to Canada, we have this advantage which we did not possess on the last occasion, that by reason of the lapse of time we are now in possession of the full report of what was said by Mr. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister of Canada, in the debate to which the noble and learned lord had made reference.
Here may I pause to say a word with respect to these misunderstandings that sometimes have arisen between the British government and our own government. The hon. member for Labelle said this afternoon it was unfortunate that any misunderstanding should arise. I agree wholly with him in that regard, and I think that every effort should be made to prevent such a possibility. But devise what plans we may for communication between governments, we are still subject to the possible misrepresentation that may come from press reports between this country and the old country, and I wish to say, after looking at the press reports which passed from this country with respect to a certain debate which took place here, and which gave rise to this discussion in the House of Lords, that I am convinced that particular discussion would never have taken place in the Lords had a correct report of the debate which took place here been sent to the paper I have in mind by its correspondent in this country.
Lord Salisbury goes on to say:
I have read the report of that speech with the greatest care, and I may say at once that His Majesty's government have no reason to complain in the least of anything which the right hon. gentleman, Mr. Mackenzie King, said on that occasion. On the contrary, I should like to bear testimony to the great courtesy
3472	COMMONS
Foreign Relations-Mr. Mackenzie King
and consideration with which he discharged the very responsible task which was thrown upon him. I have the honour of Mr. Mackenzie King's acquaintance, and I am not surprised to read that he entered into this subject with a full regard to the responsibility under which he stands and with the circumspection which the subject demands.
Elsewhere he goes on to repeat that there was this difference in the two drafts, and that I was entitled, indeed, that it was my duty, to point out the difference between them.

Would the Prime Minister permit a question? In submitting the original draft of the treaty, the British government, I presume, observed all the courtesies and requirements under the Imperial conference agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Entirely so,
yes.

And furthermore, that
treaty was not executed in any respect before it came into the hands of the Canadian government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, and as a
matter of fact it is not executed yet.
Egypt refused it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

My point was this:
There was no suggestion that the British government was seeking to commit Canada without giving the Dominion government full opportunity of considering the matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As I have said, the original draft we received admitted, to my mind, of only one interpretation, which was that we were being asked to become a party to the treaty. Apparently there were members of the British government who had no such intention in their minds. Lord Salisbury I am perfectly certain had not, from what he said. I am quite certain that Lord Salisbury would never have said in the House of Lords that that was not the intention if there had been in his mind any such intention. But what may have been in the minds of others I cannot say.

But whatever the form
was, it was submitted to us first.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, certainly, and the first form that was submitted was the form which led us to believe that we were being invited to become a party to the treaty. We made it perfectly clear that we could not accept the treaty in that form, and here may I say that I am happy to be able to inform my hon. friend the leader of the oppo-
[Mr>
Mackenzie King.]
sition, who asked earlier in the session for the correspondence, that I have received word from His Majesty's government in Great Britain which will enable me to table what is essential in the correspondence to disclose the difference, and I shall table that correspondence to-morrow.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that with respect to Egypt I have covered the point which my hon. friend the mover of the amendment had in mind. In the concluding part of his remarks he spoke more particularly of Egypt as an illustration of what might be regarded as the incurring of a moral obligation on the part of Canada through any expression on the part of our government in the nature of approval or concurrence in a matter which was submitted to us. My hon. friend referred also, I think, to Locarno, or if he did not, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), who seconded the amendment, did, and intimated that the expression of approval which was given at the Imperial conference in London of the action of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs in having succeeded in having the Locarno agreements drafted and signed was equivalent to a moral obligation on the part of Canada towards the matters referred to in those treaties, which moral obligation might grow into an act of responsibility. May I say first of all in regard to the conferences which have to be attended by members of different governments, and also in respect to communications which are submitted for the purpose of giving information, and perhaps for the purpose of receiving approval, that I cannot see how it is going to be possible to conduct conferences or correspondence between different parts of the empire if we are not to be permitted in these matters of great intematdoruatl concern the same kind of courtesies and amenities we are accustomed to use in our daily social intercourse with our neighbours. The mere fact that one gentleman expresses satisfaction at another having succeeded in doing something that is meritorious, does not to my mind involve the one who has the courtesy to convey that expression in any moral or other kind of obligation with respect to subsequent happenings. When a representative of one of the dominions moves a resolution at an Imperial conference expressing pleasure at the action of the British government or of some other government in regard to a matter that is obviously something to be pleased about, the representative of another part of the empire is put in a most invidious position indeed if he has to refrain absolutely from

, Foreign Relations-Mr. Mackenzie King
joining with his colleagues from the other dominions in that expression of good will simply because his action may be construed as involving moral obligations and obligations of a more serious character by the mere fact that he has yielded in his actions to what I would describe as a natural courtesy. Now, anything that has been done by representatives of our government at the Imperial conference which has been of the nature of a general expression of good will or appreciation of some course of conduct that has been carried' on or some achievement that has been realized by a member of the British administration, is intended to be only what on its face it purports to be, a genuine expression of good will and appreciation-nothing more; and it cannot be held to involve us in a moral or any other obligation. Similarly, if the British government or any other government of the British Empire submits to us a treaty with respect to which they think we will desire to be informed, and we give our approval or concurrence, or say that we have no objection, I hope it will be understood in all parts of the empire that what we are doing is just what we are saying and nothing more, and that any expression of good will of this character carries with it no obligation unless the obligation is specifically stated. Indeed, that is a feature of the report of the Imperial conference on treaty-making which is all-important. My hon. friend will find that the report sets out quite distinctly and deliberately that where there is an intention to bind another government by anything that is said or signed, that particular obligation must be specifically stated, and must be specifically agreed to by the government that is a consequence is to be obligated. I think tvith that understood and with that safeguard, consultation and conference and co-operation and co-ordination-all these various steps which are so essential to unity and good will between all parts of the empire-can be carried on with security and to the advantage of all concerned; but Without them even the most elemenetary discussion would, I submit, be next to impossible.
Now, my hon. friend from 'Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodtsworth) spoke of the Permanent- Court of International Justice and made special reference to the optional clause, so called. The particular paragraph of the Imperial conference report dealing with this matter is headed': Compulsory Arbitration in International Disputes. It appears at page 23 of the report, and is as follows:
One question which we studied was that of arbitration in international disputes, with special reference to the question of accentance 56103-220
of article 36 of the statute of the permanent court of international justice, providing for the compulsory submission of certain classes of eases to the court. On this matter we decided to submit no resolution to the conference, but, whilst the members of the committee were unanimous in favouring the widest possible extension of the method of arbitration for the settlement of international disputes, the feeling was that it was at present premature to accept the obligations under the article in question. A general understanding was reached that none of /the governments represented at the Imperial conference would take any action in the direction of the acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the permanent court, without bringing up the matter for further discussion.
My hon. friend said that in his opinion our government ought to notify the British government that the time has come when that matter should be brought up for discussion, and that Canada should state specifically her position thereon. Earlier in the session the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Ahshead) asked a question relating to the same matter which was answered by the Minister of Justlice (Mr. Lapointe). The question was:
I do not know whether I would be right in asking the government to make a declaration on this point. The time is getting late, and I should like the government to say something upon this point.
That is, the point referred to in the paragraph which I have just read. The Minister of Justice in reply said:
I am sorry that the hour is so late, but it is early enough for me to say simply that I am in sympathy with the subject matter of the resolution. I have some more reasons to give in support of my amendment.
The resolution moved by the hon. member for East Calgary was as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the time is opportune that according to agreement, the government of Canada should discuss with the government of Great Britain, the desirability of Canada accepting article 36 of the statutes of the Permanent Court of International Justice providing for compulsory arbitration in international disputes.
The Minister of Justice, as I have shown, was inclined to approve of the resolution and was prepared to give his reasons. In making that statement he was giving the views of the administration.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I have covered all the points that were brought up in the course of the debate. There may be others that 1 have omitted, but if so I have not done so intentionally. May I repeat to my hon. friend from Labelle what I said at the outset? I hope this reply will be sufficient to cause him not to press his motion as one of want of confidence in the administration, but rather
