Foreign Relations-Mr. Mackenzie, King
that having expressed his views, he will ask the house to permit him to withdraw the motion and that the house will give its consent.
Do I understand the Prime Minister to say definitely that on that occasion the Minister of Justice in giving his approval of the particular resolution was speaking for the government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. He always does at any time that he speaks in this house, and I think we may all rely on getting very sound opinions from him.
May I say just this word in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, because it arises out of the amendment of my hon. friend? All the matters which we have been discussing this afternoon relate more particularly to the procedure laid down at the last Imperial conference arising out of relations between the government of this dominion and the other governments of the British Empire. We have had a little over a year under the new procedure, and, so far as it is new, I should like to say that the year's experience only serves, so far as we are concerned, to confirm the wisdom of the course which at that time was taken by the Imperial conference. Particularly with respect to communications between governments I think a real advance was made when it was decided not only that communications should be direct as between the governments, but also when it was agreed that communication might be more effectively carried on if on the part of the governments concerned the personal facter were introduced. I am sure we have all been delighted at the selection which has been made by His Majesty's government in Great Britain of a high commissioner to represent that government in Canada. Sir William Clark, who will be coming to Canada in the course of the next few weeks- possibly early in September-has, as the house knows, been appointed High Commissioner in Canada for His Majesty's government in Great Britain. I believe that the opportunity for personal conference with a representative of the British government, on many matters that arise between that government and our own, will prove an effective means of avoiding possibilities of misunderstanding that occur so frequently when communications are conducted in writing. That is true with respect to communications generally as between different countries. I believe that dispatches are often written with as much regard for what is being left unsaid as for what is being said, and attention is paid to clauses and pharses and words which sometimes 6erve to make the true meaning obscure IMr_ Mackenzie King.]
indeed. Personal conference gives opportunity for all sides of a question being reviewed with care, and permits of the final drafting of a record of conversations which record is approved on both sides and admits of no misinterpretation or misunderstanding. I believe that the appointment of a high commissioner to Canada by the British government is going to be one more link which will help to ensure the continuance of the happy relations which we enjoy at the present time.
I am convinced that at no time in British history have the relations between this country and the government of Great Britain been happier or more secure than they are at this moment. And may I say further that, in my opinion, nothing in British history has done more to put the British Empire on a firm and enduring foundation than has the statement of relative position between the several governments of the empire as set forth at the Imperial conference of 1926 and as approved by all the governments there assembled.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I do not propose to trespass
long upon the time of the house. I was rather amazed that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should have suggested that those who desired to participate in the debate should do so before he replied; for the right of reply rests with the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and not with the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Before I spoke, I said.

The subject matter of
the debate has been fully canvassed in this house on previous occasions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend
is wrong; I do not think the hon. member for Labelle has any right of reply on an amendment to go into supply.	.

Pardon me, that is quite right; I was under the impression that he had moved a substantive motion. My hon. friend is right; I was treating it as a substantive motion. At any rate, the right of reply did not rest with the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not say
"reply". I said I wished to refer to the remarks of hon. members which included those of my hon. friend.

The Prime Minister's
duty was to reply to the speech of the hon. member for Labelle, who moved the amendment. His primary duty would be to do that, because the amendment is a motion of want

Foreign Relations-Mr. Bennett
of confidence in the administration and it should be spoken to either by the Prime Minister or by some other member of the administration it matters not whom.
As I have said, this matter has been fully canvassed previously in this session; much of the discussion that has taken place has already been fully covered in previous debates. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) dealt at length with the difficulties that must be experienced in giving effect to the resolutions passed at the Imperial conference of 1926. May I merely observe this: "Equality of status" is a high-sounding term, but unfortunately it cannot be said to properly represent the present position between Great Britain and the overseas dominions comprising the British Empire. Not only does it not adequately or properly represent that position, but a very great deal of work must be done before that postion is attained. As I have said on previous occasions, I regard it as a somewhat serious matter that we should be thus falsely and improperly using words-words that can have no appropriate use when applied to the present relations between Great Britain on the one hand and Canada, Australia and New Zealand on the other. How long is it desirable to continue using the wrong nomenclature? How long is it desirable to use improper terms to describe a condition? The resolution introduced by the hon. member for Labelle as an amendment to the motion to go into supply contemplates that certain action should be taken speedily; that is that speedy action should be taken to give effect to those changes that are necessary before equality of status is achieved. The resolution means that or it means nothing. It is regretted that this government has not taken those very necessary steps that must be taken if this equality is to result. That is what the resolution in terms declares. Now, I cannot think that any member on this side of the house who listened to the statements made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George in a previous debate, referring to the various statutes that must be amended and the various changes that must take place, can fail to realize that this end cannot be attained in a single day, nor in a year nor in many years; because the consents that must be secured before there is equality of status are consents that touch not only the parliament of the motherland but the parliament of every overseas self-governing dominion within the empire. That is clear; it cannot admit of doubt. The best illustration that can be used is that in connection with Egypt. Egypt was asked to sign a treaty of peace with Great Britain. The treaty was drafted and Egypt declined to execute it. Whereupon, in view 56103-2204
of the action taken by the Egyptian parliament, Great Britain made a demonstration in force for the purpose of protecting her com stitutionai rights there. Now, I put this question to every member in this house-it is a very simple question: Had war unfortunately resulted by reason of the differences of opinion between Great Britain and Egypt and a Canadian citizen'-a resident normally of Canada-had been in Cairo on that day, what would have been his position? Would he have been an alien enemy or a neutral? That is the test. There is no hon. member in this house who for a moment will say that in the eyes of international law suoh a person would be other than an alien enemy to the Egyptians. And so long as this country is not a sovereign state, it follows that it will never have equality of status with Great Britain, Whether or not this country shall be a sovereign state-which means that it must become an independent state-is a matter that must be settled by the people of Canada and not by any government in 'Canada. That is clear. For my own part I will never lift my hand to bring about that condition. I go further: for my own part I shall to the utmost of my endeavour oppose any such action, in my lifetime, that affects this Dominion. For I cannot but think that we are1 better discharging the great responsibilities that rest upon a free people, as a member of the commonwealth of nations called the British Empire, than by living a life of independence, dependent for our very existence nationally, upon the high seas and elsewhere, upon the grace and favour of powerful neighbours. That is the position I fake with respect t-o that.
But let us go a step further. Equality of status, as discussed this afternoon and this evening is, I say, a misnomer, and the case of Egypt best indicates exactly what is meant by it, but let us apply another test. There can be no equality of status as between Canada and Great Britain until both communities have the right to declare war and make peace. That is the test imposed by great writers on international law, and it does seem that without having reference to those authorities it is quite a simple one. Can Canada declare war to-day against any nation in the world? The answer must be in the negative, and so long as we may not declare war we have no equality of status with Great Britain. But if Great Britain declares war against Egypt it follows, of course, that war is thereby declared against Canada, although we may mot have been a party to any treaty made between those two countries. Our commerce would be the prize of any opposing fleet by which it might be captured; our cities might be bombarded

Foreign Relations-Mr. Bennett
and we might be driven from the world so far
as commerce and trade are concerned. That, I think, is so obvious as not to require any observations on my part other than merely to state the fact. Under these circumstances I leave it to the judgment of this house, and indeed I have stated this to others than members of this house, including imperial ministers, whether it is not very wrong and very improper to use this high sounding term with all the implications which are involved, because I know it cannot bult do harm. I agree with the Prime Minister that it is always desirable to be frank 'and open in these matters and to use words which will express one's meaning without any desire to place limitations upon them, but the words "equality of status" connote and denote a condition in this country which has not yet been reached, and a condition which may not be reached until we take a solemn step which I hope and believe we never will take and which I know we will not take in my lifetime, a step which will give Canada that right of sovereignty which it does not possess, that right to amend, aye and to make its constitution, which right we do not possess at the moment. All these changes must first be brought about, as well as changes with respect to our merchant shipping acts, with respect to the Colonial Laws Validity Acts and with respect to those innumerable statutes which have force and vigour in this Dominion, although the casual observer has no reason for believing that to be the case. These are facts which we must face, whether we like it or not, and the use of words to express a position which is not true in law and which is false in its very inception cannot do any good to these self-governing dominions.

May I ask a question?
At page 12 of the Imperial conference report there is a paragraph which covers the point to which my hon. friend is referring, as follows:
Equality of status, so far as Britain and the dominions are concerned, is thus the root principle governing our inter-imperial relations. But the principles of equality and similarity, appropriate to status, do not universally extend to function.

The hon. member for
East Calgary has made an observation which has been made before in this house. There is a frank recognition by the Imperial conference that there is no equality of status. The amendment of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) is to the effect that steps should be taken to bring about that condition and that the necessary legislative enactments should be passed by the parliament at Westminster as well ias by the parliaments of the overseas self-governing dominions. That is all that is involved in the matter at the

moment, as I see it. If I may.say so, the hon. member for Labelle was more moderate to-day in his expressions than is usually the case. I followed him with very great interest and I can only make the observation that he must not for a single moment forget that to give effect to his resolution to-day, to-morrow or next year, involves an amendment to the British North America Act so far-reaching in its consequences that I do not think many members of this house have really considered it in all its implications. If we ajre to obtain that equality of status which the hon. member apparently desires, this parliament, or shall I say the Canadian people, will have the right to create for themselves a new constitution; they will have the right to make such amendments to the present constitution as they think desirable and the struggle for confederation, which was a compromise brought about by , the far-sighted statesmanship and vision of the great men of 1867, once more will have to be thrown into the melting pot for solution. These questions are not easy of solution, and this British North America Act, which is a compromise between the views of majorities and minorities, between different races and different religions, once more will have to be proceeded' with, with everything involved thereby, before we can arrive at that happy stage to which be refers, equality of status. I cannot think that the Canadian people are disposed at this moment to forego what we have for the purpose of obtaining that of which we know not, for it involves a situation so serious, so fraught with possible disaster and so very far-reaching in its consequence and implications that I do not believe there is any body of public opinion in Canada which desires that that end should be brought about in the way I have indicated.
Therefore I venture to suggest to the hon. member in all sincerity that before he asks us to proceed immediately to bring about these constitutional changes which,- will give us that equality of status, he should seriously contemplate all that is involved in it and what the implications are; he should consider the far-reaching consequences which must follow from such action. For my own part I very much prefer this constitution in its present condition, weak though it is in many particulars, defective though it is in many instances; I prefer that rather than that we should have this straggle all over again, with its possibilities for animosities and prejudices to be aroused in this country. As I say, I prefer that constitution to this possible equality of status which would once more throw these matters into the melting pot for solution. I will not further dwell upon that

Foreign Relations-Mr. Bennett
matter, because it seems to me that it is abundantly clear to even the casual student of our constitution that the condition which we desire to bring about, some say immediately and others by slow growth and evolution, is one which has about it possibilities for evil as well as possibilities for good.
Let me go a step further. I am not seriously at variance with what has been said by the right hon. Prime Minister with respect to the severing of our relations with Russia. I heard my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) make his observations in that regard, and I cannot but think that after mature consideration and after listening to what has been said by the Prime Minister he will agree that the action taken by the head of the Canadian government was the proper action to be taken under the circumstances, and that the Prime Minister is entitled to congratulations from all rightthinking Canadians for having taken that action. After all, there can be no comity between nations when the representatives of one nation are concerned with the destruction of the government to which they are accredited. About that there can be no doubt; it is as old as the establishment of embassies; it is as old as the journeyings of ambassadors, and when the Prime Minister tells us that he was confronted by a condition such as he has alluded to to-night, I do not believe there is in any part of this country a citizen who will not be disposed to congratulate him upon the speedy action which he took and the result which was attained.
But there was one word used by my hon. friend from Labelle, or one expression, that I would wish he had not used; he spoke of our "imperial masters". I cannot but think that that was a rhetorical use of the words; I cannot think he seriously meant to imply that the people of this country were in any sense being mastered by, shall I say, our remote ancestors overseas. I am certain that is not so; I am certain there is no disposition on the part of British statesmen to indicate by thought, by word or by deed how this country should govern itself,. The Prime ministers made that abundantly clear in the discussion which took place in connection with the Egyptian treaty. It will be recalled that one who was a great prime minister of Great Britain indicated publicly that if the time should ever come when Canada let it be known that it was her desire to sever those relations light as silk and strong as steel, England would be prepared to let us go our way. I think that my hon. friend
upon reconsideration will agree that the words "his imperial masters" are not an apt designation of the relationship which now obtains between Great Britain and Canada.

I made no reference
like that in my speech this afternoon. The other day I asked in a jocose way whether the Prime Minister had received permission to deposit these documents.

One of the reasons why
I alluded to this expression was to afford my hon. friend the opportunity he has availed himself of. While the public in reading the remarks might conclude that it was a serious statement by the hon. member for Labelle, I realized that in his own consciousness he meant it in the sense in which he has now used it. I am very glad that he has taken this opportunity to give that explanation, that he had no serious thought in his mind that the people or the government of Great Britain were our imperial masters. I am sure the country will read that statement with satisfaction, and will be glad to know that it was made in a jocose sense and not in any serious sense at all.
I trust my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre will understand me when I say that it is a very dangerous thing to read a magazine article referring to the oil barons of England, France or America, and conclude that there is official sanction or authority for the conclusions or inferences which he draws from such magazine articles. The official documents referred to this afternoon by the right hon. the Prime Minister in no sense warrant the conclusion that oil barons or any other kind of barons had to do with this particular difficulty. As we all know, British capital and the capital of other nations developed the oil fields in Russia. The production of these oil wells was taken over by the Soviet government and sold without regard to the costs of development. They were enabled to obtain money for this oil, regardless of prior ownership. If you have a property to sell that cost you nothing, that you have taken from somebody else who owned it and paid for it, it is a very simple thing to compete in the markets of the world and destroy legitimate trade connections. That is the reason difficulties were experienced in Russia with respect to not only Great Britain and America, but other countries as well. To say that that had anything to do with the raid that was made upon Aroos, in London; that the literature that was found there, or the literature that was brought into this country, as mentioned by the right

Foreign Relations-Mr. Bennett
hon. the Prime Minister; that the negotiations that transpired with respect to propaganda, not only in China but in other parts of the world, had anything to do with it, is to leave a wrong impression upon the minds of those who look to members of parliament for information with respect to matters of this kind. I am satisfied that my hon. friend, steeped as his mind sometimes is in what I conceive to be unfair prejudices against capital and against those who engage in the use of money for development, has concluded that what he has read in this magazine article was the motive behind the action of the Imperial government. Having done this, I believe it is possible, but I hope not, that he has thought fit to make that the basis of the excuse for the raid that was made upon the Russian ministry in London, and for the discontinuance of official relations between Soviet Russia and this country.

Will the hon.
member not admit that the Labour party in Great Britain definitely charged that that action was taken because of matters of this character, and publicly asked for an investigation which was denied them by the Baldwin government?

It is quite correct that there are irresponsible men in England as there are even in this country, who make charges which are not warranted by facts. It is true there is a tendency to make charges against governments as the Prime Minister would say, to make a charge of lack of attention to administration, and to find excuses, if possible, which would vindicate the friendship of the Labour government with the Russian Soviet government.
The Labour government as such did not make the charges; a Labour member made the charges.
I said the Labour party, not the Labour government.
A member of the Labour party made the charges.
The leader of the Labour party.

Mr, Ramsay MacDonald is a very careful Scotchman, and while he left die impression to be drawn inferentially from his observations that the real reason for the raids upon the Russian Soviet headquarters was not the reason given by Mir. Baldwin's government, but some other reason, he was very careful not to make such a charge as would force him to stake his seat upon the authenticity or correctness of the charge. I

am sure my hon. friend will not attach too much importance to that. He is one who has sometimes said that in moments of hysteria wrong charges have been made in connection with what took place in Winnipeg some years ago, and that false inferences have been drawn and wrong conclusions have been arrived at. I am sure he did not mean to leave the impression upon this house this afternoon that it was his honest belief that anyone who had access to official sources of information would come to the conclusion that the raid made upon the Soviet headquarters by the British government was made at the behest of the oil interests of America, Great Britain and other countries. I am sure he had no such idea in his mind.

I quoted from what I regarded as a well informed article by an authority in Great Britain who definitely made those charges. I have no independent knowledge with regard to these things, and I would not expect, to find them-I think the leader of the opposition will agree with me- in official documents.

Once more I am in accord with the Prime Minister. I have no reason to believe that official documents are falsified, but I have reason to believe that the British statesmen are men of as high honour, integrity and patriotism as the man who wrote the article for the purpose of obtaining a fee from the magazine. I cannot but think that the hon. member for Labelle, who is at times rather unfortunate in attributing motives to British statesmen which I am sure were never in their minds, will agree that we must get back to the old thought that after all language is not used to disguise the thought, but rather to express the meaning which the statesmen had in their minds. As the Prime Minister has said, the ordinary amenities should be observed in these matters. I am sure that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre believes that I have sufficient confidence in his integrity and righteousness to think that he uses language to express his meaning and not to disguise it. I have every confidence that the great statesmen of Great Britain, the men who have built up this vast empire for centuries, are not men who use language to disguise their thoughts. If there were oil interests or other interests which brought about the breaking off of relations with Russia, I am sure there would be some record of it somewhere. If the British statesmen desired to say that they wanted to protect property interests of Great Britain, they would say so. They have never been reluctant to protect property interests

of Great Britain, and they have never been reluctant to express their views in that respect. They have never been slow to protect the lives of British citizens, or the property of British citizens. I accept official documents and official dispatches just as I find them, as indicating what the action was taken for and the causes given; and there is not in this house an hon. gentleman who does not believe that the causes were adequate that induced my right hon. friend's government to act in this country and that the same causes operated in Great Britain with the same result. Although we were first in point of time to complete the action that we took by dismissing the Soviet ministry from this country, although we did not raid their premises, though, as the Prime Minister said, he had that in contemplation, yet in Great Britain, acting with foresight, with knowledge, with wisdom, with a sincere and patriotic desire to serve best the interests of their country, these statesmen in their official despatches and statements represented, I believe, only the true condition of affairs and they acted in accordance with the conditions they found as indicated by those despatches and not because any oil baironis or anybody else suggested that such action should be taken.
Further, the hon. member for Labelle referred to the fact that the Secretary of State for the Dominions was of foreign birth and that he had not a drop of British blood in him. He referred to him as a Hungarian Jew. I greatly deprecate that observation . in this house and I am sure on mature deliberation the hon. member for Labelle will admit that it slipped from his tongue without his intending to give offence. One of the greatest of British Prime Ministers was a Jew and proud of the fact; but he was a British citizen and the Right Hon. Leopold Amery was bom in India, the son of a father of Devonshire, and Devonshire is a county in England. It may be that in his veins there runs some blood that may not be Anglo-Saxon; but my hon. friend should be the last to refer to that, because it is the proud boast of our country that a man is a British citizen and a British subject although, indeed, his blood may not be Anglo-Saxon, and there is no better illustration in the world of that fact than in the Dominion of Canada. That is the position with regard to that.
May I make one further observation with respect to the Egyptian treaty and I shall have concluded? I think it was very unfortunate that the Prime Minister used the words he did in the debate of the 26th

The terms of that treaty are known, they have been published. They involved military sanctions, and they contemplated military alliances. What was the reply of the government to that question? It was that we did not believe that so far as Canada was concerned the parliament of Canada would approve such a course; that if Britain and Egypt could work out a treaty as between themselves along the lines proposed, well and good; but that so far as Canada was concerned, we did not feel that it was in the interests of the British Empire itself or in the interests of the larger peace which it was hoped the treaty would serve, that this country should be asked to become a party to it; and the British government immediately accepted our view in reference thereto.
I direct the attention of the right hon. gentleman and the house to the language that is used:
The government was asked .... whether we would become a party to that treaty.
Later he said:
We were asked to become a party.
There is a vast difference between asking any person whether he will .become a party to anything and asking him to become a party. In the one instance you have the right of election and you have to say whether you will become a party or not and you consider the matter. In the other case you are asked to become a party.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I have nearly concluded all that I desire to say. The motion of the hon. member for Labelle at least clarified the situation by enabling this house once more to consider-and, I trust, to consider with some degree of care-the enormous responsibilities involved in the use of the words, "equality of status," because by implication they involve powers far-reaching and consequences that we cannot foresee. For my part I congratulate British statesmen in that they have been able during this long term of years to develop a system of communication between the various outlying sections of the empire-between the governments of the selfgoverning dominions and the motherland that have made for ease, certainty and facility in the transaction of Business. But one observation was made by the Prime Minister to-night in that regard that we cannot allow to go unchallenged. He spoke of Sir William Clark as the British High Commissioner in this country, and said that his appointment might facilitate the transaction of business between this country and Great Britain. It must not be forgotten that whatever difficulties there may be with regard to notes and despatches passing between the government of the motherland and the government of Canada, in the ultimate analysis, either by cable or by written communication, the High Commissioner of Great Britain must send his messages to the government that accredits him. And so it always has been. The written word sometimes is much more reliable and avoids misunderstandings to which conversations sometimes give rise. I recall reading not long since an account of what took place in 1891 at Washington, when a misunderstanding arose between Mr. Blaine and two of His

Foreign Relations-Mr. Bennett
Majesty's commissioners from Canada as to what had been said, and it brought about considerable difficulty. Conversations in diplomacy have caused difficulties, and any member of this house who has read what transpired in connection with the great war will realize the different views given by German statesmen and British statesmen as to certain conversations that had taken place, and volumes have been written about such misunderstandings. So recourse is had to despatches, to written communications, as the ultimate authority upon which nations rely to govern and guide their policies. While the introduction to Canada of a British High Commissioner may serve a useful purpose for parole communications, yet in the end written communications must govern.
We on this side of the house have already indicated that the very appointment of a Canadian minister at. Tokyo will be wholly misunderstood by the oriental mind, for it predicates to the world that we are a sovereign state. As I read in the previous debate from great authorities on international law, that means, if it means anything, that we are a sovereign state; which we are not. The very appointment of such a minister, with the possibility of difficulties and differences in respect to foreign policy, involves implications, as I said before, most serious in their consequences. I do not think the people of this country are desirous of having ministers in foreign countries unless they are certain that those ministers on grave matters of foreign policy, whjch may mean life or death to the great empire of which we are proud to be a member, will co-ordinate their views with the views of the British ambassador. To have a representative working with the ambassador of Great Britain is one thing; but to have a minister who at any time may differ with the views expressed by the British ambassador may bring about an impossible situation in the life of the empire. If hon. gentlemen have in mind the ultimate thing which is involved by implication in what is being put forward, that is, that we shall assert our mind and carry it to its ultimate conclusion, regardless of the expressions of opinion by His Majesty's ambassador who may be present in the very same capital, well and good; but let us face it frankly and not use words to disguise our thoughts and endeavour to skate around the position which we are to take. That is the stand which we on this side of the house take in this matter.
I shall not discuss the proposed Tokyo embassy because an opportunity will be presented during the presentation of the estimates

for the Department of External Affairs to deal with it fully, except in a few words to express our attitude with respect to it. speakeroldname: Mr. J. T. THORSON (Winnipeg South Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the speeches which have been delivered on this very interesting question. The hon.	member for	Laibelie	(Mr. BouraSsa) has moved an amendment to the motion to go into supply and has expressed regret that the Canadian government has not taken adequate	steps to	implement	the
declaration of equality of status pronounced at the Imperial conference of 1926.
Last session I spoke at some length on the status of Canada, confining myself to a discussion of the autonomy of Canada in her domestic affairs.	To-night	I	welcome	the
opportunity of discussing her status in so far as external affairs and international relations are concerned. I am of the opinion that whatever may be the status of Canada in so far as her domestic affairs are concerned, there has been a fundamental change in her international status. Her separate status in that sphere has been recognized not only by Great Britain but by other great world powers. This international! recognition, of our separate status is the strongest possible evidence of its existence. I think it would be wise to review the constitutional developments that have taken place in recent years, particularly during the last decade. It might well be called a decade of constitutional development; indeed, it might well be described as one of the most important decades in the history of Canada. Each year has its events of outstanding importance. I propose therefore to review these events very briefly so that we may have before us a panorama of the progress that has taken place. This will enable us to see Clearly what has happened and to appreciate fully what the present situation really is.

Foreign Relations-Mr. Thorson
In 1949 the peace treaty of Versailles was signed. Sir Robert Borden, then Prime Minister of Canada, insisted that Canada should sign that treaty, and he finally prevailed upon Great Britain to endorse the propriety of that step. There was great opposition from the American delegation led by President Wilson and Mr. Lansing. To them this suggestion was an unheard of departure from international usage and practice. But Cle-menceau, in his blunt way, pointed out that there were as many Canadian soldiers lying in the fields of France as there were Americans; that Canada had taken her part in the war and should have the right to take part in the negotiations leading to peace. This view eventually prevailed. This was Canada's first international recognition. It is true that this international recognition of Canada was a mark of courtesy rather than a fact of any juridical importance; for the British Empire signed that treaty and, in so signing it, bound all of the self-governing dominions. Sir Robert Borden also in that year obtained for Canada separate representation in the assembly of the League of Nations, and the right to have the Canadian representative eventually elected to the council of the league. This was Canada's first adventure in the arena of international politics, and it had for its primary object the promotion of world peace. The senate of the United States objected very strongly to the separate voting power of the dominions in the assembly of the league.
Then in 1920 the proposal that Canada should have a minister plenipotentiary at Washington was announced. On May 10, 1920, Sir George Foster, who was Acting Prime Minister, made the following announcement to the House of Commons:
It has been agreed that His Majesty, on idvice of his Canadian ministers, shall appoint 1 minister plenipotentiary who will have charge of Canadian affairs and will at all times be the ordinary channel of communication with the United States government in all matters of purely Canadian concern, acting upon instructions from and reporting direct to the Canadian government. In the absence of the ambassador the Canadian minister will take charge of the whole embassy and of the representation of imperial as well as Canadian interests. He will be accredited by His Majesty to the president -with the necessary powers for the purpose.
Sir George Foster added the following to this announcement:
This new arrangement will not denote any departure either on the part of the British government or of the Canadian government from the principle of the diplomatic unity of the British Empire.
There may be a very great difference of opinion as to the correctness of this conclusion. It has been suggested by many students of constitutional law that this proposal, together with the signature of Canada to the peace treaty, and Canada's separate representation in the assembly of the League of Nations, marked the beginning of the disintegration of the diplomatic unity of the empire. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who were then members of the opposition, objected to the proposal that the Canadian minister should take charge of imperial affairs, and suggested that he should be independent of the British embassy and concern himself solely with Canadian affaire. For over six years no action was taken to implement the arrangement that was proposed to this parliament in 1920.
In 1921 the question of Canadian representation at the Washington disarmament conference came up. President Harding had summoned a conference between the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy and Japan to discuss disarmament. 'General Smuts of South Africa had objected to the action of the American government in addressing its invitation to the British government alone, ignoring the dominions, and had cabled to the Canadian Prime Minister protesting that, in view of the agitation in the American senate against the independent voting power of the dominions in the League of Nations, it was a direct challenge to the new dominion status and it would be a bad precedent for the dominions to attend without having been properly invited, but if a stand were made the battle for their international recognition and international status would be finally won. Mr. Meighen, who was then Prime Minister of Canada, thereupon communicated with the British Prime Minister, and it was finally agreed that the status of the Dominion representatives at the Washington conference should be exactly the same as it had been at the peace conference at Versailles. Canada was represented at the Washington peace conference by Sir Robert Borden. His powers to represent the Dominion were issued by the crown on an order in council of the Canadian cabinet.
In 1922 the Washington conference was held, in the month of January. At that conference the British delegation spoke with one voice, as it had done at Versailles, after consultation amongst its own members. Subsequently the Italian government extended an invitation to an international conference at Genoa, this invitation being addressed by the

The present Prime Minister took the view- and I suggest that it was a very sound view to take-that the question of sending a Canadian contingent was for the Canadian parliament alone to decide. He intimated that he would be very glad to receive the fullest information in order to decide upon the advisability of summoning parliament. If the Prime Minister was too modest to claim that his action had a great deal to do with averting war, I have no hesitation in expressing my personal opinion that it had that effect. On February 2, 1923, the Prime Minister made a statement in the House of Commons, and I challenge any hon. member of this house to deny the propriety of the sentiments he then expressed. He said:
-if the relations between the different parts of the British empire are to he made of an enduring character, this will only be through a full recognition of the supremacy of parliament, and this particularly with regard to matters which may involve participation in war.
This was an assertion in forcible language of Canadian autonomy in so far as active participation in war is concerned. In my opinion it was also, in a sense, a repudiation of a central foreign policy, in which Canada did not concur.
The year 1923 was one of great importance so far as our constitutional development was concerned. I shall deal very briefly with three events which took place in that year, the Lausanne conference, the Halibut treaty and the Imperial conference. Canada refused to accept the special responsibilities of the Lausanne treaty because Canada was not a party to the negotiations. In the course of a statement made to the House of Commons on April 2, 1924, the Prime Minister explained the attitude of Canada in these words:
We take the position that, not having been invited to the Lausanne conference, not having

been represented there, not having for the reasons that I have mentioned, signed the treaty, the treaty does not impose obligations on Canada, and that the parts of the empire on which it does impose obligations are the only parts that should be expected to sign and ratify it. As we did not regard the treaty as imposing obligations on Canada, we did not feel that it was necessary to submit the treaty to parliament for its approval, or in its name to signify concurrence in its ratification.
This was a fresh declaration of autonomy in external affairs, and a restatement of the right of parliament to determine Canada's policy, going even a step further than was taken in the previous year. If I were to interject a personal note, I think I might accurately say that the sentiments expressed with regard to the Chanak incident and the Lausanne conference found some echo in the famous speech delivered by Mr. Meighen at Hamilton prior to the Bagot by-election.
The Halibut treaty was signed at Washington on March 2, 1923, by Mr. Lapointe, then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, on behalf of Canada. That was the first time a treaty had been made with a foreign country, having to do with Canadian affairs, which was signed by a Canadian minister without the intervention of the British ambassador. In my opinion it marked a great advance in Canadian treaty making powers. Later on I shall refer again to this treaty. The United States senate took exception to some of the terms of that treaty, suggesting that they should be made applicable to all British subjects rather than confined to Canadian nationals, but eventually these objections were withdrawn and the treaty was ratified by the senate of the United States early in 1924.
The Imperial conference of 1923 was another event of outstanding importance, particularly with regard to the resolutions passed by it relating to the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties. The conference of that year ratified and approved the precedent established by Canada in connection with the halibut treaty and asserted the right of the dominions to negotiate and sign treaties involving themselves only without the intervention of the British ambassador. This marked a further breach in the doctrine of diplomatic unity, and a great advance was made in the direction of complete autonomy over external affairs and in international relations. A greater advance was to take place in 1926. After the Imperial conference of 1923 I think I am safe in saying that the theory of a joint foreign policy for all the constituent parts of the British. empire suffered a very marked modification.

In 1924 the Canadian government objected to the manner of representation at the international conference called to devise means of carrying out the Dawes plan of reparations, and suggested that the representation at that conference should follow the precedent set at Versailles and Washington, under which our Dominion would be separately represented by its delegate bearing full powers from His Majesty the King to act in the name of His Majesty in respect of the Dominion. Senator Belcourt was sent to that conference as the Canadian representative.
In 1925 there were two events of considerable importance. The International Boundary Treaty was made in that year with the United States in the name of His Majesty the King in respect of the Dominion of Canada. It was negotiated and signed by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) without the intervention of the British ambassador and without any objection being made by the United States. Then came the famous Locarno treaty of that year, which contained an important clause which had not been included in all previous treaties. That clause was to the effect that the treaty should impose no obligation upon any of the British dominions or upon India unless the government of such dominion or of India should signify its acceptance. Great Britain refused to sign that treaty, as did Canada, but our refusal to sign was based upon very different grounds from those taken by Great Britain. Once again Canada refused to accept any commitments resulting from a treaty which had been made without any co-operation on her part. There was this difference between the Locarno treaty and the Lausanne treaty: the latter, having been made in the name of the British empire, notwithstanding the protests raised by the present Prime Minister bound all the dominions, while the Locarno treaty specifically exempted those portions of the empire which did not accept the treaty.
The year 1926 was perhaps the most important year since confederation in respect to the constitutional development of Canada. It saw a new status conferred upon Canada in so far as external affairs are concerned, and oomplete international recognition of that new status. In that year the Canadian minister to Washington was appointed. The proposal of 1920 was ultimately carried into effect, with this very important difference, that the Canadian minister to Washington is not a member of the British embassy but is there as the representative of Canada concerned only with Canadian affairs. All negotiations 'between the United States government and the Canadian government pass through him as our Canadian representative there.
I propose to discuss only one feature of the report brought down by the Imperial conference, that portion of the report which deals with the making of treaties. Prior to 1926 treaties were made between His Majesty and foreign powers in the - name of the British Empire, or by His Majesty the King without stating for whom the treaty was made. Therefore, such treaties bound the whole empire including all of the dominions, unless the dominions were expressly excepted from their terms, as would have been the case had the Locarno treaty been adopted. In that sense, of course, the Lausanne treaty was binding upon Canada, notwithstanding the refusal of the Canadian parliament to accept its responsbilities or to admit its active obligations. In the same way, the Halibut treaty was binding upon Great Britain and the other dominions, in the sense that it was a treaty between His Majesty, to whom all the dominions owe allegiance, and the United States, and was not made in respect of any particular dominion.
The old practice of making treaties underwent a very important change. Treaties to which His Majesty the King is a party are all made by His Majesty the King, but they are now made only in respect of those portions of the British Empire that are to be bound by them. The Imperial conference recognized the right of each dominicfn to make separate independent treaties which would not be binding upon any other member of the British family of nations. Treaties will now be made by His Majesty the King only in respect of those portions of the empire which wish to be parties to them. In each case the king will issue full powers to his plenipotentiaries to negotiate and sign treaties, and these full powers will be issued upon the advice of the government concerned, indicating the part of the empire for which they are to sign.
For example, if a treaty is not to be binding upon any of the dominions, it will be made by His Majesty the King and it will state on the face of it that it is made "for the United Kingdom, of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and all parts of the empire which are not separate members of the League of Nations." Such a treaty will, on the face of it, be a very different treaty from the Lausanne treaty and other treaties that have been made, for not even in international law will such a treaty bind the dominions.

I do not know who the next ambassador is going to be or whither he is to go. Some countries are left yet. Obviously all those who desire appointments cannot get into the Senate, because there are not enough vacancies; nor can they all get on the bench. There are fifty-five applications a paper says for junior county court judgeships in Winnipeg alone. If anybody wants any of these jobs he has to pay his dollar and join the ward association. I suppose these ambassadors have paid their dollar and joined the Liberal ward associations also. Why, in my riding there are gentlemen who have canvassed me, one looking for a judgeship and another for an ambassadorship. I saw one of them here in the halls the other day. Evidently they fancy I have some influence with this government. One gentleman who ran against me lost his deposit; he lost the election only by about 10,000 or 12,000 votes. And I did not have even one ambassador to vote for me. The only ambassador I have ever had the honour of representing used to live in a former constituency of mine, North Toronto, but he
is now in England. I refer to Mr. P. C. Larkin. No doubt under the new status regime

this magnificent new regime that has been ushered in-ambassadorships will be found for all those who want them, but they must pay a dollar and join the ward association. The hon. member for LaJbelle might be made ambassador extraordinary to France, and he is certainly extraordinary; there is no doubt about that-to France or Italy or some place like that. That is the place for him. He is not satisfied with the way they do things in New France. He is a nationalist. But I want to say that it takes more than gentlemen like the hon. member for Labelle -it takes more than men of his nationalist stripe-to make a nation. No doubt in a few days when parliament closes, if this resolution goes through, we shall see the hon. gentleman from Labelle on the high seas taking Cook's tour as our new ambassador to France. One of these gentlemen, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), has already gone to the League of Nations to bring about peace over there. He could not pacify a few steelworkers who were on strike in the city I come from; yet he has gone abroad to pacify Europe. I understand that a good many of them are going to take this Cook's tour. One or two of them go by way of Halifax and Quebec, but the rest of these gentlemen always sail from New York on American liners, that is the new status way of patronizing Canadian ports. That is the way they do things under this magnificient new status regime. I do not know who will be the new ambassador to Tokyo or to China; nor have I any idea as to whether the proposed ambassador to China can talk Chinese, status or not. I do not know whether he can say in Chinese "I want my laundry", or "Is my laundry ready?" I suppose, though, when he goes over there, under this very splendid new status regime that has been introduced, and in the magnificent style that now obtains, he will hold five o'clock teas and ten o'clock dinners for the Chinamen. No doubt our ambassador to China will hold pink teas and invite all the Chinese aristocracy. He will invite these Chinese to his social functions: "Will you have pink tea with me this afternoon?" "Thanks; I will Mr. Ambassador. I believe in equality of status; so do you."
The Prime Minister of Australia came to Canada after the last Imperial conference and he gave certain addresses in this country, speaking before the Canadian clubs. And by the way, may I observe here that some of our Canadian clubs are no more Canadian than some of the Empire clubs are imperial. However, as I say, that gentleman gave addresses

Foreign Relations-Mr. Church
in Canada on the results of the Imperial conference to the oversea dominions, and he was severely called down by the Prime Minister of this country who in effect practically told him to mind his own business. This was in reference to what Australia and New Zealand had done at the Imperial conference. Those two dominions at the Imperial conference, instead of whining from the housetops about their status, instead of complaining about this, that and the other, went prepared with an economic brief, and were willing to sit at the round table and discuss things, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier did when he represented the people of this country at similar conferences. Canada cannot expect to do all the talking in the empire, to suggest all the imperial policies for the motherland, and have the British taxpayer shoulder the cost of defending the empire. Why should Canada do all the talking and shouting from the housetops and the mother country-the British taxpayer-foot the bill? Yet that is what it amounts to under this magnificent new equality of status regime we have to-day.
The pacifist and the nationalist are much alike; the pacifists are for the new status, and so are the nationalists. I am a good Canadian nationalist, Mr. Speaker, because I am a true British imperialist. I do not want this country to enjoy the fruits of freedom and have the British taxpayers pay for the protection which our commerce is given on the high seas. A true Canadian nationalist will not want Canada to appear before the rest of the world as a pauper in this regard. But that is the position that Canada will occupy if this changed status is brought about. Canada is not a nation and never was a nation; we are part and parcel of the British Empire and shall continue to be, though we had a carload of gentlemen like the hon. member for Labelle prepared to state otherwise. There are many problems which should have been taken up at the Imperial conference and which were not there discussed.
Has the hon. member concluded?
No, Mr. Speaker.

It is eleven o'clock and I wish to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
